questions.stem: A business laptop must join the company's Active Directory domain, be encrypted with BitLocker, and have settings pushed via the local Group Policy Editor. What is the MINIMUM Windows 10/11 edition that supports all three?

explanation.correct: Domain join, BitLocker, and gpedit.msc all first appear in Windows Pro, so Pro is the minimum edition that meets every requirement.

distractors.A: Enterprise also qualifies but is volume-licensed with extras (AppLocker, DirectAccess); it is more than the minimum.
distractors.C: Pro for Workstations supports them but adds ReFS, more RAM/CPU sockets and server-grade features you don't need — it exceeds the MINIMUM.
distractors.D: Home cannot join a domain, has no BitLocker, and ships without the Local Group Policy Editor — it fails all three needs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Home = consumer (no domain join, no BitLocker, no gpedit). Pro = business baseline. Enterprise/Education = volume-licensed with the extras.

questions.stem: After installing a new webcam, a technician sees it listed with a yellow exclamation mark indicating a driver problem. Which built-in Windows tool is used to view and manage hardware devices and their drivers?

explanation.correct: Device Manager lists installed hardware and its drivers; a yellow '!' flags a device with a driver/resource issue you can update or roll back there.

distractors.B: Event Viewer displays system/application logs; it records events but doesn't manage devices.
distractors.C: Task Manager shows running processes, startup apps and performance — not hardware drivers.
distractors.D: Disk Management creates/formats partitions and volumes, not device drivers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hardware + drivers = Device Manager (devmgmt.msc); yellow '!' = driver/resource problem.

questions.stem: Windows is behaving oddly and a technician suspects corrupted protected system files. From an elevated Command Prompt, which command scans those files and automatically repairs them?

explanation.correct: System File Checker (sfc /scannow) verifies the integrity of protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted ones from a cached copy.

distractors.A: diskpart is an interactive partition/volume manager; it doesn't repair system files.
distractors.B: gpupdate /force reapplies Group Policy settings — unrelated to file corruption.
distractors.C: chkdsk /f fixes file-system errors on a disk volume, not corrupted OS system files.

explanation.exam_pattern: Corrupt system files = sfc /scannow; disk/file-system errors = chkdsk; deeper image repair = DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth.

questions.stem: A user needs to copy a single 12 GB video file onto a USB flash drive and read/write it on both Windows and macOS. Which file system should the drive be formatted with?

explanation.correct: exFAT has no practical 4 GB file-size cap and is read/write on both Windows and macOS, making it ideal for large files on cross-platform removable media.

distractors.A: FAT32 caps individual files at 4 GB, so it cannot hold a 12 GB file.
distractors.B: NTFS handles large files but macOS mounts it read-only by default, breaking cross-platform write.
distractors.C: ext4 is a Linux file system that Windows and macOS do not natively read or write.

explanation.exam_pattern: exFAT = large files + cross-platform (Win/mac) flash media; FAT32 capped at 4 GB files; NTFS = Windows.

questions.stem: A technician is performing a clean install of Windows 11 on a new 4 TB drive and wants to use the entire capacity and boot in UEFI mode with Secure Boot. Which partitioning scheme must the drive use?

explanation.correct: GPT supports volumes larger than 2 TB and is required to boot Windows in native UEFI/Secure Boot mode, so it uses the full 4 TB.

distractors.A: exFAT is a file system, not a partition scheme, so it doesn't answer this.
distractors.B: Dynamic disk is a Windows disk TYPE (vs basic) for spanning/mirroring; it's unrelated to UEFI booting a 4 TB drive.
distractors.C: MBR tops out at 2 TB and 4 primary partitions, and pairs with legacy BIOS boot — it can't use the full drive.

explanation.exam_pattern: UEFI + drives > 2 TB = GPT; legacy BIOS/MBR caps at 2 TB and 4 primary partitions.

questions.stem: From a Windows command line, a technician needs to map the shared folder \\fileserver\projects to drive letter S:. Which command does this?

explanation.correct: net use <drive>: <UNC path> maps a shared network folder to a drive letter from the CLI.

distractors.A: netstat displays active connections and listening ports; it doesn't map drives.
distractors.C: nslookup queries DNS name resolution; it can't mount a share.
distractors.D: net user creates and manages local/domain user accounts — it does not map drives.

explanation.exam_pattern: Map a network drive from CLI = net use <letter>: \\server\share.

questions.stem: A macOS user accidentally deleted a document last week and wants to restore the earlier version using Apple's built-in backup utility. Which feature should they use?

explanation.correct: Time Machine is macOS's automatic backup tool; the user can browse back in time to a previous date and restore the deleted file.

distractors.B: Mission Control arranges open windows, spaces and desktops — it doesn't recover files.
distractors.C: Spotlight is the system-wide search feature, not a backup/restore tool.
distractors.D: Disk Utility formats, partitions and repairs disks (First Aid); it is not a file backup system.

explanation.exam_pattern: macOS: Time Machine = backups, Spotlight = search, Disk Utility = format/repair, Keychain = passwords.

questions.stem: On a Linux workstation a user downloaded a shell script named deploy.sh and needs to make it executable before running it. Which command accomplishes this?

explanation.correct: chmod changes a file's permission bits; +x adds the execute permission so the script can be run.

distractors.A: ls -l only LISTS a file's permissions and details — it shows them but changes nothing.
distractors.B: chown changes the file's OWNER, not its execute permission.
distractors.D: grep searches for text patterns within files; it doesn't set permissions.

explanation.exam_pattern: chmod = change permissions (+x execute); chown = change owner; ls -l shows permissions.

questions.stem: A secure login requires a password plus a one-time code generated by an authenticator app on the user's phone. Which two categories of authentication factors does this use?

options.text: Something you know and something you are
Something you know and something you have
Something you are and something you do
Something you have and somewhere you are

explanation.correct: The password is 'something you know' and the authenticator app on the phone is 'something you have,' so this is true multifactor authentication.

distractors.A: 'Something you are' is a biometric (fingerprint, face) — no biometric is used here.
distractors.C: 'Something you do' is a behavioral factor (gesture, typing rhythm); neither it nor a biometric is used.
distractors.D: 'Somewhere you are' is a location/geolocation factor, which isn't part of this login.

explanation.exam_pattern: Factors: know (password/PIN), have (token/phone/smart card), are (biometric). MFA = two or more DIFFERENT categories.

questions.stem: A user's documents are now inaccessible and an on-screen message demands payment in cryptocurrency in exchange for a key to unlock them. Which type of malware is this?

explanation.correct: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files and demands payment (often in cryptocurrency) for the decryption key — exactly the behavior described.

distractors.A: A keylogger secretly records keystrokes to steal credentials, not encrypt data for ransom.
distractors.C: A rootkit hides itself and maintains stealthy privileged access; it doesn't ransom files.
distractors.D: Spyware covertly gathers information about the user; it doesn't lock files for payment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Files encrypted + payment demand = ransomware; hidden admin-level persistence = rootkit; captured keystrokes = keylogger.

questions.stem: An unauthorized person slips through a badge-secured door by walking in closely behind an employee who just swiped their card. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured entry point without presenting your own credentials.

distractors.A: Dumpster diving is searching discarded trash for useful information.
distractors.B: Phishing uses fraudulent messages to trick victims into revealing information or clicking links.
distractors.C: Shoulder surfing is secretly watching someone enter a password or PIN, not following them through a door.

explanation.exam_pattern: Following someone through a secure door = tailgating; a mantrap/access control vestibule is the classic countermeasure.

questions.stem: A user's account has Full Control NTFS permission on a shared folder, but the Share permission for their group is set to Read. The user opens the folder from another PC across the network. What is their effective permission?

explanation.correct: When a resource is reached over the network, Windows applies the MORE restrictive of the combined NTFS and Share permissions. Full Control (NTFS) vs Read (Share) resolves to Read.

distractors.B: The user does have access — Read — so 'No access' is wrong.
distractors.C: Full Control is only the NTFS side; the Read share permission overrides it for network access.
distractors.D: Modify is neither of the two permissions in play and isn't the intersection of them.

explanation.exam_pattern: Network access: effective permission = the MORE restrictive of combined NTFS vs combined Share. Local access ignores Share permissions.

questions.stem: A technician is hardening shared lab workstations against malware and unauthorized access. Which TWO actions improve the security posture? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disable Windows Defender Firewall on all machines
Add every lab user to the local Administrators group
Enforce a strong password policy with account lockout

explanation.correct: Disabling AutoRun stops malware on inserted USB drives from launching automatically, and a strong password policy with lockout resists guessing/brute-force — both harden the system.

distractors.A: Turning off the firewall removes a protective control and WEAKENS security — the opposite of hardening.
distractors.C: Making everyone a local administrator violates least privilege and lets any user (or their malware) change the system.

explanation.exam_pattern: Harden = disable AutoRun, enforce strong passwords/lockout, patch, least privilege. Never 'harden' by disabling the firewall or handing out admin.

questions.stem: A hospital must guarantee that data on failed magnetic hard drives is unrecoverable before the drives leave the building, and the drives will NOT be reused. Which method is the MOST appropriate?

options.text: Overwriting once, then redeploying the drives
Deleting the files and emptying the Recycle Bin

explanation.correct: Shredding physically destroys the platters so data can never be recovered, and the drive is not reused — the right choice when disposal and certainty are required.

distractors.B: A single overwrite then redeploy is sanitization for REUSE, but the requirement is destruction with the drive not reused and removed from the building.
distractors.C: A quick format only clears the file table; the underlying data remains and is recoverable.
distractors.D: Deleting files and emptying the Recycle Bin removes pointers only — the data is trivially recoverable.

explanation.exam_pattern: Physical destruction (shred/drill/incinerate/degauss) = unrecoverable & not reused; wiping/overwrite = sanitize for REUSE; format/delete are NOT secure.

questions.stem: A Windows PC began throwing frequent blue screens (BSOD/STOP errors) immediately after the user installed a new graphics driver. What is the BEST first step to resolve it?

options.text: Boot into Safe Mode and roll back the graphics driver in Device Manager
Perform a clean reinstall of Windows

explanation.correct: The crashes started right after the driver change, so rolling back the driver (from Safe Mode if Windows won't stay up) directly undoes the likely cause.

distractors.A: Defragmentation addresses disk fragmentation/performance, not driver-induced STOP errors.
distractors.C: Reinstalling Windows is drastic and premature when a simple driver rollback likely fixes it.
distractors.D: Replacing hardware is unjustified; nothing points to a failed motherboard, and the trigger was a driver.

explanation.exam_pattern: BSOD right after a driver/update change -> roll back the driver/update (Safe Mode if needed) before drastic steps.

questions.stem: A Windows 10 PC takes a very long time to reach the desktop because too many applications launch at boot. Which tool lets the technician disable unnecessary startup programs?

explanation.correct: In Windows 10/11 the Startup tab of Task Manager lists auto-start programs and lets you disable them (msconfig's Startup tab now redirects here).

distractors.A: Disk Management handles partitions and volumes, not startup applications.
distractors.C: Windows Defender is antivirus/antimalware; it doesn't control the startup program list.
distractors.D: Device Manager manages hardware and drivers, not which programs launch at boot.

explanation.exam_pattern: Manage startup programs in Win10/11 = Task Manager > Startup (msconfig's old job).

questions.stem: Following CompTIA's best-practice procedure for malware removal, a technician has just investigated and verified the malware symptoms on a PC. What is the NEXT step?

options.text: Enable System Restore and create a restore point

explanation.correct: After verifying symptoms, the next step is to quarantine the infected system so the malware cannot spread while you work on it.

distractors.A: Educating the end user is the FINAL (7th) step, done after the system is clean.
distractors.C: Scheduling scans and running updates is step 5, part of ongoing remediation — not immediately after identification.
distractors.D: You DISABLE System Restore early (step 3); re-enabling it and creating a restore point is step 6, near the end.

explanation.exam_pattern: Malware 7 steps: Investigate -> Quarantine -> Disable System Restore -> Remediate -> Schedule scans/update -> Re-enable System Restore -> Educate.

questions.stem: On one user's PC, many HTTPS websites throw 'Your connection is not private' / invalid certificate errors, yet the same sites load fine on other computers. What should the technician check FIRST?

options.text: Whether every one of those websites is down at once
Whether the router needs a firmware update
The PC's system date and time

explanation.correct: An incorrect system clock makes valid certificates appear expired or not-yet-valid, so TLS validation fails across many sites — and the problem is isolated to that one PC.

distractors.A: Every one of those sites being down simultaneously is implausible and would affect all computers, not just one.
distractors.B: A router firmware issue would affect all devices on the network, not cause cert errors on a single PC.
distractors.D: A failing keyboard has nothing to do with certificate trust errors.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cert 'not valid / not private' errors on many sites but one PC only -> check that PC's date/time first.

questions.stem: A company smartphone suddenly has very poor battery life, feels hot even when idle, and shows a spike in cellular data usage. The technician suspects a rogue app. What is the BEST first step?

options.text: Review per-app battery and data usage in Settings and uninstall the suspicious app
Perform a factory reset before investigating

explanation.correct: The battery/data usage screens pinpoint which app is consuming resources, so you can uninstall the offending app — a targeted, least-invasive first step.

distractors.B: Disabling cellular permanently breaks the phone's purpose and doesn't remove the rogue app.
distractors.C: A factory reset is a last resort and wipes user data; investigate and remove the app first.
distractors.D: Swapping the battery ignores the symptom pattern (overheating + data spike) that points to software.

explanation.exam_pattern: Mobile: fast drain + overheating + data spike -> check per-app battery/data usage and uninstall the rogue app before wiping.

questions.stem: A new technician asks for the exact, repeatable step-by-step instructions the team follows to image and configure a new laptop. Which type of document provides this?

explanation.correct: A standard operating procedure documents the agreed, repeatable steps for a task so everyone performs it consistently.

distractors.A: A EULA states the legal terms for using software; it is not a work procedure.
distractors.C: A topology diagram maps how devices connect on the network, not how to perform a task.
distractors.D: An incident report records the details of a specific event after it happens.

explanation.exam_pattern: Step-by-step 'how we do X' = SOP; map of the network = topology diagram.

questions.stem: Before a major server upgrade is submitted to the change advisory board, management asks what the team will do if the upgrade fails in production. Which element of the change request answers this?

explanation.correct: The rollback/back-out plan documents how to revert the systems to their previous working state if the change fails.

distractors.A: Risk analysis weighs the likelihood and impact of problems, but doesn't itself specify the reversal steps.
distractors.C: Purpose explains WHY the change is being made, not what to do if it fails.
distractors.D: Scope defines which systems/users the change affects, not how to undo it.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'What if it breaks?' = rollback/back-out plan. Scope = what's touched; risk analysis = what could go wrong.

questions.stem: A company runs a full backup every Sunday. Each weekday it then backs up only the data changed since the LAST backup of any type and clears the archive bit, keeping nightly backups as fast as possible. Which backup type runs on weekdays?

explanation.correct: An incremental backup captures only what changed since the last backup of ANY type and clears the archive bit — fast to back up, but a restore needs the full plus every increment.

distractors.A: A full backup copies all data every time — that's the weekly job, not the quick nightly one.
distractors.B: A synthetic full is assembled from existing backups on the backup server; it isn't the daily changed-data job described.
distractors.C: A differential backs up everything changed since the last FULL and does NOT clear the archive bit, so it grows larger each day.

explanation.exam_pattern: Incremental = since last backup (any), fast backup/slow restore, clears archive bit. Differential = since last FULL, grows daily, restore = full + one diff. (See also the 3-2-1 rule.)

questions.stem: A technician is about to replace RAM and an expansion card inside a desktop. Which TWO practices help prevent electrostatic discharge (ESD) damage to the components? (Choose two.)

options.text: Wear an anti-static wrist strap connected to a grounding point
Touch the gold edge connectors and chips directly to 'ground' them
Store and transport the components in anti-static bags
Work while standing on a carpeted floor

explanation.correct: An anti-static wrist strap keeps you at the same potential as the chassis, and anti-static bags protect parts from static while handling/storing them — both reduce ESD risk.

distractors.B: You should handle cards by their edges and AVOID touching the gold contacts and chips, which is where ESD does its damage.
distractors.D: Carpet generates static charge; working on it INCREASES the chance of ESD, not reduces it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Prevent ESD: anti-static wrist strap + mat, anti-static bags, raise humidity, handle boards by the edges; avoid carpet and touching contacts.

questions.stem: A technician discovers illegal content on a company computer that may become evidence in a legal case. Documenting every person who handles the drive, and when, from seizure through to court, is known as what?

explanation.correct: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who controlled the evidence and when, preserving its integrity and admissibility.

distractors.A: An acceptable use policy defines how employees may use company resources.
distractors.B: A rollback plan is a change-management concept for reverting a failed change.
distractors.D: A knowledge base article is reference documentation for solving known issues.

explanation.exam_pattern: First responder: identify, report through proper channels, preserve the data/device, and document the chain of custody.

questions.stem: A frustrated customer is venting at length about a recurring problem. Which response best demonstrates professional communication?

options.text: Listen actively without interrupting, acknowledge the issue, then explain the next steps
Tell them it's not your department and end the call
Put them on hold and complain about the 'silly' issue to a coworker
Interrupt to correct them and point out what they did wrong

explanation.correct: Actively listening, not interrupting, showing empathy, and clearly explaining next steps are core professional-communication behaviors.

distractors.B: Brushing the customer off and abandoning the call fails to meet or set expectations.
distractors.C: Mocking a customer, even on hold, is unprofessional and breaches basic courtesy.
distractors.D: Interrupting and blaming the customer is dismissive and escalates frustration.

explanation.exam_pattern: Professionalism: actively listen, don't interrupt, be empathetic, avoid jargon, and set/meet expectations.

questions.stem: A technician saved an automation script with a .ps1 file extension. Which scripting environment is this file intended for?

explanation.correct: The .ps1 extension identifies a Windows PowerShell script.

distractors.A: Python scripts use the .py extension.
distractors.C: Bash shell scripts use the .sh extension.
distractors.D: Windows batch files use .bat (or .cmd), not .ps1.

explanation.exam_pattern: .ps1 PowerShell | .bat/.cmd batch | .sh Bash | .py Python | .vbs VBScript | .js JavaScript.

questions.stem: While working a help-desk ticket, a technician records a running, timestamped account of each action taken as the issue is being resolved. Which ticket field is being filled in?

explanation.correct: Progress notes capture the ongoing, step-by-step actions taken while the ticket is being worked, keeping a clear record for hand-offs and audits.

distractors.A: The problem description is the initial statement of the reported issue, written when the ticket is opened.
distractors.C: Categories classify the type of issue (e.g., hardware, email) for routing and reporting.
distractors.D: Severity rates how urgent/impactful the issue is; it does not record the work performed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ticket fields: problem description (initial) -> progress notes (ongoing work) -> problem resolution (final fix); severity/categories classify it.

questions.stem: An organization attaches a unique barcoded label to every laptop and records its serial number, purchase date, and warranty status in a central database. This practice is BEST described as what?

options.text: Asset management using asset tags and an inventory database

explanation.correct: Asset tags/barcodes plus an inventory database that tracks procurement, warranty, and assignment are the core of asset management.

distractors.A: An SOP documents the repeatable steps for performing a task.
distractors.B: An AUP defines how employees may use company resources; it is not an inventory record.
distractors.D: A topology diagram maps how devices connect on the network, not an inventory of owned equipment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Asset tags/barcodes + inventory database (serial, procurement, warranty) = asset management.

questions.stem: Which organizational policy specifies the minimum length, required complexity, and how often users must change their sign-in credentials?

explanation.correct: A password policy defines credential rules — minimum length, complexity, history, and rotation/expiration intervals.

distractors.B: An incident response policy defines how security incidents are reported and handled.
distractors.C: An MDM policy governs enrollment and control of mobile devices (encryption, remote wipe, app restrictions).
distractors.D: An AUP states how employees may use company systems and data, not password rules.

explanation.exam_pattern: Credential length/complexity/rotation rules = password policy; resource-use rules = AUP.

questions.stem: After solving an unusual printer error, a technician writes up the symptoms and the fix and adds it to a shared, searchable repository so colleagues can reuse the solution later. What is this repository called?

explanation.correct: A knowledge base is a searchable collection of articles documenting known issues and their resolutions so solutions can be reused.

distractors.A: A topology diagram maps the network's connections.
distractors.C: An SOP lists the agreed, repeatable steps for performing a task, not a record of a specific solved issue.
distractors.D: A change request is a formal proposal to modify a system.

explanation.exam_pattern: Searchable repository of known issues + fixes = knowledge base/articles.

questions.stem: In a formal change-management process, which group reviews a proposed change and formally approves or rejects it before it is implemented?

options.text: The end users who will be affected

explanation.correct: The change advisory board (change board) evaluates the request, weighs the risk, and gives the formal approve/reject decision before implementation.

distractors.A: Vendor support may advise, but it is not the organization's change-approval authority.
distractors.C: The incident response team handles security incidents, not change approvals.
distractors.D: Affected end users provide acceptance and feedback, but they do not formally authorize the change.

explanation.exam_pattern: Formal body that approves/rejects a change = change advisory board (CAB).

questions.stem: Before rolling a configuration change out to production, a team first applies and tests it in an isolated environment that mirrors production but cannot affect live systems. What is this environment called?

explanation.correct: Sandbox testing applies the change in an isolated, production-like environment first, so problems are found without risking live systems.

distractors.B: A production baseline is the documented known-good production configuration, not a test area.
distractors.C: A change request is the formal proposal document that describes the change.
distractors.D: A backout plan is the documented steps to revert if the change fails — not the place you test it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Isolated, test-before-deploy environment = sandbox testing.

questions.stem: A change plan is technically ready, but before scheduling the rollout the project lead confirms that the affected department has reviewed the change, agrees with it, and is prepared for it. Which change-management element does this satisfy?

explanation.correct: End-user acceptance confirms the people affected have reviewed and agreed to the change and are ready for it before it goes live.

distractors.A: Sandbox testing validates the change in an isolated environment, not with the users.
distractors.B: Risk analysis evaluates the likelihood and impact of problems to assign a risk level.
distractors.D: The backout plan describes how to revert the change if it fails.

explanation.exam_pattern: Affected users review and agree before rollout = end-user acceptance.

questions.stem: A consultant recommends following the 3-2-1 backup rule. What does this rule require?

options.text: Keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy off-site
Run 3 daily, 2 weekly, and 1 monthly backup job
Keep 3 full backups, 2 incrementals, and 1 differential each week
Retain backups for 3 years, test 2 of them, and encrypt 1

explanation.correct: The 3-2-1 rule means keep at least 3 copies of your data, store them on 2 different media/storage types, and keep 1 copy off-site.

distractors.B: This invents a job frequency; the numbers in 3-2-1 refer to copies/media/off-site, not jobs per period.
distractors.C: This mixes up backup types; the rule is about copies, media, and location, not a weekly type schedule.
distractors.D: Retention, testing, and encryption are good practices but are not what 3-2-1 defines.

explanation.exam_pattern: 3-2-1 = 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 copy off-site.

questions.stem: A company has run nightly backups for a year but has never confirmed that the backups can actually be restored. Which practice directly addresses this gap?

options.text: Regularly test and verify restores from the backups
Switch from full to incremental backups
Move all backups onto the same server as the production data
Increase the backup frequency to hourly

explanation.correct: Backups are only useful if they restore. Periodically performing test restores verifies the media and the backup chain are actually recoverable.

distractors.B: Changing the backup type does not demonstrate recoverability.
distractors.C: Co-locating backups with the production data violates off-site/3-2-1 and risks losing both at once.
distractors.D: More frequent backups still prove nothing about whether a restore will succeed.

explanation.exam_pattern: A backup you've never restored isn't proven — test/verify restores on a schedule.

questions.stem: A backup scheme keeps separate daily, weekly, and monthly backup sets, promoting certain backups to longer retention as they age. This rotation scheme is known as what?

explanation.correct: Grandfather-father-son rotates media across daily (son), weekly (father), and monthly (grandfather) sets, balancing retention against the number of tapes/media.

distractors.A: Chain of custody is an evidence-handling record in incident response, unrelated to backup rotation.
distractors.B: The 3-2-1 rule governs how many copies, how many media types, and off-site storage — not a retention rotation.
distractors.D: A synthetic full is a full backup assembled on the backup server from earlier backups; it is a type, not a rotation scheme.

explanation.exam_pattern: Daily/weekly/monthly retention rotation = Grandfather-Father-Son (GFS).

questions.stem: A power supply bursts into flames while it is still plugged in and energized. Which class of fire extinguisher is designed for electrical equipment fires?

explanation.correct: Class C extinguishers are rated for energized electrical equipment; they use a non-conductive agent so the operator isn't shocked.

distractors.A: Class D is for combustible metals such as magnesium or lithium.
distractors.B: Class B is for flammable liquids and gases.
distractors.D: Class A is for ordinary combustibles like wood, paper, and cloth.

explanation.exam_pattern: Energized electrical fire = Class C (A=ordinary combustibles, B=liquids, D=metals).

questions.stem: A technician is decommissioning old gear. Which TWO items must be handled as regulated/toxic waste and taken to an approved recycling or disposal facility rather than placed in the regular trash? (Choose two.)

options.text: A used laser printer toner cartridge

explanation.correct: Batteries and toner are regulated/hazardous materials; both must be recycled or disposed of per the SDS and local regulations, not thrown in the trash.

distractors.C: A plastic drive-bay blank is inert plastic and is not regulated waste.
distractors.D: An anti-static bag is ordinary plastic packaging with no hazardous content.

explanation.exam_pattern: Regulated/toxic waste: batteries, toner, and CRTs -> recycle/dispose per the SDS and local regulations.

questions.stem: Before handling and disposing of a chemical cleaning solvent, a technician needs to know its hazards, required protective equipment, and proper disposal steps. Which document provides this information?

explanation.correct: A safety data sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) documents a substance's hazards, safe-handling and PPE requirements, storage, and disposal instructions.

distractors.A: A EULA states the legal terms for using software.
distractors.C: An AUP defines how employees may use company resources.
distractors.D: An SOP lists repeatable task steps; it is not the authoritative source for a chemical's hazards.

explanation.exam_pattern: Chemical hazards/handling/PPE/disposal info = SDS (formerly MSDS).

questions.stem: A technician must move a heavy UPS from the floor up to a rack. Which lifting technique is safest?

options.text: Bend at the waist and lift using the back muscles
Twist at the waist while carrying the load to set it down
Bend at the knees and lift with the legs, keeping the back straight and the load close
Hold the load at arm's length to keep it away from the body

explanation.correct: Lift with the legs, keep the back straight and the load close to the body to avoid back injury; get help or a cart for heavy items.

distractors.A: Lifting with the back rather than the legs is the classic cause of lifting injuries.
distractors.B: Twisting while loaded is a common way to injure the back; turn with your feet instead.
distractors.D: Holding the load away from the body greatly increases strain on the back.

explanation.exam_pattern: Personal safety: lift with the legs, back straight, load close, don't twist; observe weight limits.

questions.stem: A technician is the first to discover a possible security incident on a user's PC. Following first-response best practice, what should they do?

options.text: Post a warning in the company chat so everyone is aware
Report it through the proper channels and preserve the data/device
Immediately wipe the drive to stop the threat from spreading
Keep using the PC to investigate the problem on their own

explanation.correct: First response is to identify the incident, report it through the proper channels, and preserve the affected data/device so evidence stays intact.

distractors.A: Broadcasting the incident can violate policy and tip off a malicious insider; use proper channels.
distractors.C: Wiping the drive destroys the very evidence an investigation needs.
distractors.D: Continuing to use the device can alter or destroy evidence and should be avoided.

explanation.exam_pattern: First response: identify -> report through proper channels -> preserve the data/device (don't alter/destroy).

questions.stem: When collecting digital evidence from a running computer, which data should be captured FIRST because it is lost soonest?

options.text: Printed documents in a filing cabinet
The contents of RAM and the list of running processes
Files stored on the hard drive

explanation.correct: The order of volatility says to collect the most volatile data first — CPU cache and RAM (running processes, network connections) vanish when power is lost.

distractors.A: Printed documents are the least volatile of all and are not time-sensitive to capture.
distractors.C: Backup tapes are archival and change least often — among the last to collect.
distractors.D: Disk data is far more persistent than memory, so it is collected after volatile memory.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order of volatility: capture most volatile first (CPU cache/RAM) before disk, then backups/archives/printouts.

questions.stem: A healthcare provider stores patients' medical histories and treatment records. Which category of regulated data is this, requiring special handling and protection?

explanation.correct: Medical and treatment records are protected health information (PHI), a regulated data class (e.g., under HIPAA) with strict handling requirements.

distractors.A: PCI covers cardholder/payment card data governed by PCI DSS, not medical records.
distractors.B: Source code is intellectual property but is not one of the regulated-data categories (PII/PCI/GDPR/PHI).
distractors.C: Public marketing material is not sensitive or regulated data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Regulated data: medical = PHI, card data = PCI, personal identifiers = PII, EU personal data = GDPR.

questions.stem: A user wants to install one purchased, single-seat copy of a program on 15 office computers, but the license forbids it. Which concept governs how many installations and what use are permitted?

options.text: The software license / EULA (enforced by DRM)

explanation.correct: The end-user license agreement (EULA) and the license type define how many installs and what usage are allowed; digital rights management (DRM) enforces it. Installing a single-seat license on 15 PCs violates it.

distractors.A: Chain of custody is the documented handling of evidence in an investigation.
distractors.C: The change advisory board approves changes; it does not set license terms.
distractors.D: An AUP governs how employees may use resources, not software license counts.

explanation.exam_pattern: How many installs / what use is allowed = software license/EULA (personal vs enterprise, open-source vs commercial); DRM enforces it.

questions.stem: While explaining a repair to a non-technical customer, which communication practice is MOST professional?

options.text: Avoid jargon, acronyms, and slang and explain in plain language
Use as many technical acronyms as possible to show expertise
Rush through the explanation so the customer isn't bored
Tell the customer the details are too complex to explain

explanation.correct: Matching your language to the audience — avoiding jargon, acronyms, and slang — keeps a non-technical customer informed and respected.

distractors.B: Piling on acronyms confuses a non-technical customer and signals poor communication.
distractors.C: Rushing fails to confirm understanding and to set/meet expectations.
distractors.D: Dismissing the customer as unable to understand is condescending and unhelpful.

explanation.exam_pattern: Professionalism: avoid jargon/acronyms/slang; speak to the customer's level.

questions.stem: Which TWO behaviors reflect professional conduct while working at a customer's workspace? (Choose two.)

options.text: Arrive on time, and contact the customer if you will be delayed
Silence your phone and avoid personal calls, texting, and social media
Take personal calls at the desk so you stay reachable
Post the customer's problem on social media to crowdsource a fix

explanation.correct: Being on time (or calling ahead) and avoiding personal distractions are core professional behaviors on site.

distractors.C: Taking personal calls is a distraction that undermines professionalism and focus.
distractors.D: Posting a customer's issue on social media discloses private information and breaches confidentiality.

explanation.exam_pattern: Professionalism: be on time (or call), avoid distractions, and never disclose customer info on social media.

questions.stem: While repairing a manager's laptop, a technician notices personal financial documents and private emails open on the screen. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Copy them in case they are needed later as evidence
Read through them to check whether they relate to the repair
Mention the interesting ones to coworkers afterward
Keep the materials confidential — do not access, copy, or share them

explanation.correct: Confidential and private materials must be left alone — a technician should not access, copy, or share a customer's private data.

distractors.A: Copying private materials without authorization is inappropriate and a privacy violation.
distractors.B: Reading private documents that aren't relevant to the task violates the customer's privacy.
distractors.C: Gossiping about a customer's private information is a serious breach of professionalism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Deal appropriately with confidential/private materials: don't access, copy, or share them.

questions.stem: A legacy Windows logon script is written in Microsoft's VBScript language. Which file extension identifies it?

explanation.correct: VBScript files use the .vbs extension.

distractors.B: .js identifies a JavaScript file.
distractors.C: .sh identifies a Linux/Unix Bash shell script.
distractors.D: .py identifies a Python script.

explanation.exam_pattern: .vbs VBScript | .js JavaScript | .py Python | .sh Bash | .ps1 PowerShell | .bat/.cmd batch.

questions.stem: An administrator needs every workstation to automatically reconnect a shared network drive at each user logon. Which is the BEST use of scripting here?

options.text: A logon script that remaps the network drive automatically
Replacing the file server with a cloud storage subscription
Emailing users instructions to map the drive themselves
Manually mapping the drive on each PC every morning

explanation.correct: Remapping network drives is a classic scripting use case — a logon script does it automatically and consistently for every user.

distractors.B: Swapping out the file server is an unrelated infrastructure change, not the automation requested.
distractors.C: Relying on users to follow emailed steps is inconsistent and generates support calls.
distractors.D: Manually mapping each PC daily does not scale and is error-prone.

explanation.exam_pattern: Scripting use cases: remap drives, restart machines, install apps, automate backups, gather info, push updates.

questions.stem: Before deploying a script across many machines, which TWO are legitimate risks a technician should weigh? (Choose two.)

options.text: Inadvertently changing system settings or crashing the system/browser
Permanently voiding the device's hardware warranty
Making the script impossible to edit once it is saved

explanation.correct: Scripts can carry or fetch malware, and a flawed script can inadvertently change system settings or exhaust resources and crash the system or browser.

distractors.B: Running a script does not void a device's hardware warranty.
distractors.D: Scripts are plain text and remain freely editable after they are saved.

explanation.exam_pattern: Script risks: introducing malware, inadvertently changing system settings, and system/browser crashes from mishandling resources.

questions.stem: A remote employee must connect INTO their office PC using Remote Desktop (RDP) so the office machine acts as the host that accepts the incoming session. What is the MINIMUM Windows 10/11 edition the office PC needs?

explanation.correct: Hosting incoming Remote Desktop sessions (the RDP server role) first appears in Windows Pro, so Pro is the minimum edition for the office PC.

distractors.B: Home can only run the Remote Desktop CLIENT (connect OUT); it cannot accept incoming RDP sessions, so it can't be the host.
distractors.C: Pro for Workstations also hosts RDP but adds server-grade hardware/ReFS support you don't need here.
distractors.D: Enterprise can host RDP but is volume-licensed with extra features — it exceeds the MINIMUM.

explanation.exam_pattern: Any Windows edition can be an RDP CLIENT; only Pro and above can be the RDP HOST.

questions.stem: A developer wants to run virtual machines using the hypervisor that is built into Windows rather than installing a third-party product. Their PC currently runs Windows 11 Home. What is the MINIMUM edition that includes this built-in hypervisor?

explanation.correct: Client Hyper-V, the hypervisor built into Windows, is available starting in Windows Pro (64-bit), so Pro is the minimum edition that provides it.

distractors.A: Enterprise also includes Hyper-V but exceeds the minimum Pro requirement.
distractors.C: Windows Home does NOT include Hyper-V; the feature isn't present to turn on.
distractors.D: Education includes Hyper-V but is a volume-licensed edition beyond the minimum.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hyper-V (client) = Pro / Enterprise / Education / Pro for Workstations — never Home.

questions.stem: A workstation has 16 GB of RAM physically installed, but the System page reports only about 3.5 GB is usable and the OS cannot address more. Which is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The edition is Windows Home, which caps RAM at 4 GB
One memory module is faulty and must be replaced
BitLocker reserves the remaining RAM for encryption
A 32-bit (x86) version of Windows is installed

explanation.correct: A 32-bit edition of Windows can address only about 4 GB of memory total (~3.2-3.5 GB usable), so extra installed RAM is ignored. Moving to 64-bit Windows removes the limit — which requires a clean install, not an in-place change.

distractors.A: Windows Home (64-bit) supports up to 128 GB, not 4 GB — the edition isn't the cap here.
distractors.B: A faulty module would reduce total RAM but wouldn't impose a clean ~4 GB addressing ceiling the way an x86 OS does.
distractors.C: BitLocker encrypts the drive and does not reserve gigabytes of RAM.

explanation.exam_pattern: ~4 GB usable ceiling regardless of installed RAM = 32-bit (x86) Windows; 32->64-bit needs a clean install.

questions.stem: An engineering workstation needs the ReFS file system, support for up to 4 physical CPU sockets, and very large RAM capacity (up to 6 TB). Which Windows edition is specifically designed to provide this high-end hardware and resilient-storage support?

explanation.correct: Pro for Workstations targets high-end hardware: it supports ReFS, up to 4 CPU sockets and up to 6 TB of RAM (plus persistent memory and SMB Direct).

distractors.B: Pro supports only 2 CPU sockets and up to 2 TB RAM and does not create ReFS volumes.
distractors.C: Enterprise is volume-licensed for management/security features but still supports only 2 CPU sockets — not the 4-socket workstation hardware.
distractors.D: Home is a consumer edition (1 socket, 128 GB RAM cap) and far below these needs.

explanation.exam_pattern: ReFS + 4 CPU sockets + 6 TB RAM = Pro for Workstations; Pro caps at 2 sockets / 2 TB and no ReFS.

questions.stem: A technician wants Windows to restart directly into Safe Mode on the next boot using the built-in GUI utility whose Boot tab has a 'Safe boot' checkbox. Which tool should they open?

explanation.correct: System Configuration (msconfig) has a Boot tab with a 'Safe boot' option that forces the next restart into Safe Mode.

distractors.B: services.msc starts/stops Windows services — it has no boot-mode setting.
distractors.C: regedit edits the registry directly; it isn't the GUI for choosing a Safe Mode boot.
distractors.D: Task Manager manages processes and startup apps; the Safe boot option lives in msconfig, not here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Safe boot / boot options = msconfig (Boot tab). Startup apps moved to Task Manager; services = services.msc.

questions.stem: After a PC reboots unexpectedly, a technician wants to review timestamped System and Application error and warning entries that Windows logged. Which built-in tool displays these logs?

explanation.correct: Event Viewer stores Windows Logs (System, Application, Security, etc.) with timestamps and severity, the right place to review errors after a crash.

distractors.A: Performance Monitor graphs live and logged performance counters, not system event logs.
distractors.B: Device Manager manages hardware/drivers; it doesn't display System/Application logs.
distractors.C: Task Manager shows current processes and resource use, not the historical event log.

explanation.exam_pattern: Review logged events = Event Viewer; live performance = Performance/Resource Monitor; hardware = Device Manager.

questions.stem: A newly installed second SSD does not appear in File Explorer. Which built-in Windows tool is used to bring the disk online, initialize it, and create and format a new volume with a drive letter?

explanation.correct: Disk Management initializes new disks and creates, formats and assigns drive letters to volumes, which makes the SSD usable and visible in File Explorer.

distractors.A: System Information (msinfo32) is a read-only summary of the system — it changes nothing on disk.
distractors.C: Disk Cleanup removes temporary files to free space; it doesn't initialize or format disks.
distractors.D: Device Manager confirms the disk's driver/hardware is recognized but does not create or format volumes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Initialize/partition/format/assign letters = Disk Management (GUI) or diskpart (CLI).

questions.stem: On Windows 10/11, which built-in tool has a Startup tab that shows each startup program's 'Startup impact' and lets you enable or disable it (functionality that moved here from System Configuration)?

explanation.correct: Since Windows 8, startup-app management (with a 'Startup impact' rating) lives on the Task Manager Startup tab, where you can disable unneeded auto-start programs.

distractors.B: regedit can show Run keys but has no 'Startup impact' rating or simple enable/disable toggle.
distractors.C: msconfig's Startup tab now just links out to Task Manager; the actual control moved there.
distractors.D: services.msc manages background services, which are different from per-user startup applications.

explanation.exam_pattern: Startup apps = Task Manager (Startup tab) in Win8+; msconfig still owns boot options, not startup apps.

questions.stem: A website changed its IP address, but one workstation still connects to the old address because of a stale cached name resolution. Which command clears the local DNS resolver cache?

explanation.correct: ipconfig /flushdns empties the local DNS resolver cache, forcing a fresh lookup that picks up the new IP address.

distractors.A: ipconfig /all only displays the full IP configuration; it changes nothing.
distractors.C: ipconfig /release drops the current DHCP lease (IP address); it doesn't touch the DNS cache.
distractors.D: ipconfig /renew requests a new DHCP lease; it doesn't clear cached DNS records.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stale name resolution = ipconfig /flushdns; DHCP lease issues = /release then /renew.

questions.stem: A technician suspects an aging hard drive has physical bad sectors. Which command locates bad sectors and attempts to recover any readable information (while also fixing file-system errors)?

explanation.correct: chkdsk /r locates bad sectors and recovers readable information; it implies /f, so it fixes file-system errors too.

distractors.A: chkdsk /f fixes file-system errors but does NOT scan the surface for bad sectors.
distractors.B: format erases the volume and recreates the file system — it destroys data rather than recovering it.
distractors.C: sfc /scannow repairs protected Windows system files, not disk sectors.

explanation.exam_pattern: /f = fix file-system errors; /r = /f PLUS locate bad sectors and recover readable data.

questions.stem: sfc /scannow reports that it found corrupt files but 'was unable to fix some of them.' Which command repairs the underlying Windows component store so a follow-up sfc run can succeed?

explanation.correct: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth repairs the component store (the source sfc copies known-good files from), so re-running sfc afterward can complete repairs.

distractors.B: sfc /verifyonly only checks integrity and reports; it makes no repairs.
distractors.C: chkdsk /r fixes disk/file-system problems and bad sectors, not the Windows image/component store.
distractors.D: bootrec /fixmbr repairs the master boot record for boot problems — unrelated to corrupt system files.

explanation.exam_pattern: sfc can't fix it -> DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then run sfc /scannow again.

questions.stem: A technician needs to copy a folder AND all of its subfolders from the Windows command line. Which TWO commands can copy a directory tree including subdirectories? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: robocopy (robust file copy) copies directory trees and is the modern tool, and xcopy /E copies folders including subdirectories (even empty ones).

distractors.A: move relocates files/folders (and deletes the source); it is not a copy command.
distractors.D: copy transfers individual files only — it cannot recurse into subdirectories.

explanation.exam_pattern: Copy directory trees = robocopy (preferred) or xcopy /E (/S excludes empty dirs); copy = single files.

questions.stem: A user's group is granted the share permission 'Read' on a folder, while the NTFS permission for that group on the same folder is 'Modify.' When the user opens the folder OVER THE NETWORK, what is their effective permission?

explanation.correct: Over the network both share and NTFS permissions apply, and the effective result is the MOST RESTRICTIVE of the two. Share Read is more restrictive than NTFS Modify, so the user gets Read.

distractors.A: Modify is the NTFS level, but the Read share permission caps network access below it.
distractors.C: Full Control is granted by neither permission here.
distractors.D: Access isn't denied — Read is allowed; logging on locally would even bypass the share and give Modify.

explanation.exam_pattern: Share + NTFS over the network = most restrictive wins; local logon ignores share permissions.

questions.stem: When a standard user launches a program that needs to make system changes, Windows dims the screen and prompts for administrator approval or credentials before continuing. Which feature produces this prompt?

explanation.correct: User Account Control (UAC) uses the secure (dimmed) desktop to request consent or admin credentials before an action that requires elevation proceeds.

distractors.A: Windows Defender Firewall filters network traffic, not application elevation.
distractors.C: BitLocker encrypts drives; it doesn't produce elevation consent prompts.
distractors.D: EFS encrypts individual files per user; it isn't the elevation prompt mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Dimmed secure desktop + admin consent prompt = UAC (elevation).

questions.stem: A user wants to encrypt a few specific files and folders on an NTFS volume so that only their Windows account can read them, without encrypting the entire drive. Which feature should they use?

explanation.correct: EFS encrypts individual files/folders on NTFS, tied to the user's account key, so only that user can decrypt them — exactly per-file, per-user protection.

distractors.A: BitLocker encrypts an ENTIRE volume, not selected files for a single user.
distractors.C: BitLocker To Go encrypts entire REMOVABLE drives, again not individual files on a fixed disk.
distractors.D: NTFS compression reduces file size; it provides no encryption or access protection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Per-file/per-user encryption = EFS (NTFS); whole-volume encryption = BitLocker (removable = BitLocker To Go).

questions.stem: Before installing a questionable driver, a technician wants a quick way to later roll back system files, drivers, and the registry to an earlier point WITHOUT affecting the user's documents. Which Windows feature provides this?

explanation.correct: System Restore (part of System Protection) creates restore points that revert system files, drivers, and the registry to an earlier state while leaving personal files alone.

distractors.A: Disk Cleanup frees space by deleting temporary files; it can't roll the system back.
distractors.B: Reset this PC reinstalls Windows (optionally removing everything) — far more drastic than a rollback.
distractors.D: File History backs up and restores personal files/versions, not system files or the registry.

explanation.exam_pattern: Roll back system state, keep user files = System Restore point; back up user files = File History.

questions.stem: Windows is misbehaving due to corrupted system files, but the user must keep all of their installed applications and personal files. Which installation approach meets this requirement?

options.text: In-place upgrade (repair installation) of the same Windows version
Format the drive and reinstall Windows

explanation.correct: An in-place upgrade / repair installation reinstalls Windows over itself, refreshing system files while preserving installed applications and user data.

distractors.A: A clean (custom) install wipes the partition and keeps no apps or settings.
distractors.C: Formatting and reinstalling destroys all apps and data on the volume.
distractors.D: 'Remove everything' deletes personal files and apps — the opposite of what's required.

explanation.exam_pattern: Keep apps + files while repairing = in-place upgrade/repair install; clean install = wipe and start fresh.

questions.stem: An administrator must deploy Windows to 50 new PCs that have blank drives and no installation media, pulling the OS image from a deployment server over the LAN as each PC powers on. Which boot method accomplishes this?

explanation.correct: PXE (Preboot eXecution Environment) lets a network-enabled PC boot from a deployment server over the LAN, ideal for imaging many machines with no local media.

distractors.A: USB boot still requires physically inserting media into every PC, defeating 'no media.'
distractors.B: A recovery partition restores a single existing machine; new blank drives have none.
distractors.D: Optical boot requires a disc in each machine and an optical drive — not a network deployment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Image many diskless/new PCs from a server over the network = PXE boot.

questions.stem: To make Windows Setup run without prompting a technician — automatically supplying the language, product key, partition choices, and account settings — which item provides those answers for an unattended installation?

explanation.correct: An unattended install uses an answer file (unattend.xml, named autounattend.xml on boot media) that supplies the responses Setup would otherwise prompt for.

distractors.B: A WIM (Windows Imaging Format) file stores the captured OS image; it holds files, not the setup answers.
distractors.C: An FFU (Full Flash Update) image is a sector/disk image used to flash a drive — not the answer source.
distractors.D: An ISO is the installation media container; by itself it doesn't automate the prompts.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automate Setup prompts = answer file (unattend.xml/autounattend.xml); WIM/FFU = image formats.

questions.stem: A user connects a Windows laptop to Wi-Fi at a coffee shop. Which network location profile should be selected so the laptop is NOT discoverable and file/printer sharing stays off?

explanation.correct: The Public profile hides the device from network discovery and keeps sharing off — the correct choice on untrusted networks like a coffee shop.

distractors.B: Private is for trusted home/work networks and ENABLES discovery and sharing.
distractors.C: Domain is applied automatically only when the PC is joined to an Active Directory domain.
distractors.D: Metered is a data-usage setting to limit background traffic, not a discovery/sharing profile.

explanation.exam_pattern: Untrusted network = Public (not discoverable); trusted = Private; AD-joined = Domain (automatic).

questions.stem: A 500-employee company wants centralized user logon accounts and policies managed from a server so settings apply to every PC. Which Windows networking model supports this centralized management?

explanation.correct: A domain uses Active Directory on a domain controller for centralized accounts and Group Policy, scaling to hundreds or thousands of managed PCs.

distractors.A: HomeGroup was a simple home file/printer-sharing feature (now removed), not centralized enterprise management.
distractors.B: A workgroup is peer-to-peer with separate local accounts on each PC — no central management, best for small groups.
distractors.D: Public is a firewall/network-location profile, not an account-management model.

explanation.exam_pattern: Centralized accounts + Group Policy on a server = Domain; peer-to-peer local accounts = Workgroup.

questions.stem: A technician wants other users on the trusted (private) LAN to reach a printer that is attached to a Windows PC. In Advanced sharing settings, which TWO options must be turned on? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set the network profile to Public

explanation.correct: Turning on File and printer sharing exposes the shared printer, and Network discovery lets other PCs find the computer on the network so they can connect to it.

distractors.A: A metered connection limits background data usage; it has nothing to do with printer sharing.
distractors.D: Setting the profile to Public would HIDE the PC and block sharing — the opposite of the goal.

explanation.exam_pattern: Share on a private LAN = enable Network discovery + File and printer sharing (and allow it through the firewall).

questions.stem: On a Mac, a downloaded app from an 'unidentified developer' is blocked from opening by default. Which macOS security feature enforces that only signed/notarized or App Store apps run unless the user overrides it?

explanation.correct: Gatekeeper checks an app's signature/notarization and, by default, blocks apps from unidentified developers until the user explicitly allows them.

distractors.B: FileVault is macOS full-disk encryption — it doesn't gate which apps may launch.
distractors.C: Time Machine is the backup utility, unrelated to app signing checks.
distractors.D: Keychain stores passwords, keys and certificates; it isn't the app-launch gatekeeper.

explanation.exam_pattern: macOS app-launch allow/block by signature = Gatekeeper; disk encryption = FileVault.

questions.stem: A MacBook user wants built-in full-disk encryption so that data cannot be read if the laptop is lost or stolen. Which macOS feature provides this?

explanation.correct: FileVault encrypts the entire startup disk (XTS-AES), so the data is unreadable without the account password/recovery key if the Mac is stolen.

distractors.A: Mission Control arranges windows, spaces and desktops — unrelated to encryption.
distractors.C: Disk Utility formats, partitions and repairs disks (First Aid); it doesn't encrypt the whole system disk on its own.
distractors.D: Gatekeeper controls which apps are allowed to launch, not disk encryption.

explanation.exam_pattern: macOS full-disk encryption = FileVault (Windows equivalent = BitLocker).

questions.stem: On a Debian/Ubuntu-based Linux system, which command installs a software package along with its dependencies from the configured repositories?

explanation.correct: apt-get (or apt) is the package manager for Debian/Ubuntu; 'apt-get install <pkg>' downloads and installs a package and its dependencies from the repositories.

distractors.A: yum (and dnf) is the package manager for Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS family systems, not Debian/Ubuntu.
distractors.C: grep searches text within files/output; it is not a package manager.
distractors.D: chmod changes file permission bits; it installs nothing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Debian/Ubuntu = apt/apt-get; Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS = yum/dnf.

questions.stem: On Linux, a script should be readable, writable, and executable by its owner, and only readable and executable by the group and everyone else (rwxr-xr-x). Which chmod numeric (octal) mode sets exactly this?

explanation.correct: Each digit sums read(4)+write(2)+execute(1): owner rwx = 7, group r-x = 5, others r-x = 5, giving 755 (rwxr-xr-x).

distractors.A: 644 is rw-r--r-- (no execute for anyone) — the script could not be run.
distractors.C: 777 is rwxrwxrwx, granting write to group and others as well — too permissive.
distractors.D: 750 is rwxr-x--- which removes all access for 'others,' not read+execute as required.

explanation.exam_pattern: Octal permissions: r=4, w=2, x=1 per owner/group/other. rwxr-xr-x = 755; rw-r--r-- = 644.

questions.stem: A technician tries to open the Local Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc) to tighten a setting on a user's Windows 11 Home laptop, but Windows reports it cannot find gpedit.msc. What is the MOST likely reason?

options.text: The user is not signed in with a Microsoft account
gpedit.msc only launches from Safe Mode
The laptop must be joined to a domain before gpedit will run
The Local Group Policy Editor is not included in the Home edition

explanation.correct: gpedit.msc ships only with Pro and higher editions. Windows Home has no Local Group Policy Editor, so the file genuinely isn't present.

distractors.A: A Microsoft vs. local account has no bearing on whether gpedit.msc exists.
distractors.B: gpedit does not depend on Safe Mode — it simply isn't installed in Home.
distractors.C: Domain join is itself a Pro+ capability; Home can't join a domain, and gpedit is a LOCAL tool that doesn't require one anyway.

explanation.exam_pattern: Home edition lacks gpedit.msc, BitLocker, domain join, and the RDP host role — those require Pro, Pro for Workstations, or Enterprise.

questions.stem: A video-editing workstation has 256 GB of RAM installed, but 64-bit Windows Home cannot use all of it. Which edition change lets Windows address far more memory (up to 2 TB)?

options.text: No Windows edition supports more than 128 GB of RAM
Switch the PC into S mode
Reinstall Windows Home as the 32-bit version

explanation.correct: 64-bit Windows Home caps at 128 GB of RAM; Windows Pro raises the ceiling to 2 TB (Pro for Workstations and Enterprise go to 6 TB), so a Pro upgrade lets the 256 GB be used.

distractors.A: False — Pro supports 2 TB and Pro for Workstations/Enterprise 6 TB.
distractors.B: S mode locks the PC to Store apps for security; it does not raise RAM limits.
distractors.C: 32-bit Windows can address only ~4 GB total — far worse, not better.

explanation.exam_pattern: 64-bit RAM ceilings by edition: Home 128 GB, Pro 2 TB, Pro for Workstations/Enterprise 6 TB. 32-bit any edition ≈ 4 GB.

questions.stem: An administrator is choosing Windows editions for office desktops that MUST join the corporate Active Directory domain. Which TWO editions support joining a domain? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Domain join is available in Pro, Pro for Workstations, and Enterprise. Pro and Enterprise are the two listed that qualify.

distractors.A: Home cannot join a domain — it must first be upgraded to Pro.
distractors.C: Home Single Language is a Home variant and also cannot join a domain.

explanation.exam_pattern: Domain join = Pro / Pro for Workstations / Enterprise. No Home edition can join an Active Directory domain (workgroup only).

questions.stem: A user bought a PC preloaded with Windows 11 Home and now needs BitLocker and the ability to join the company domain, WITHOUT reinstalling or losing data. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Download a third-party tool to add domain join to Home
Enable the features in Control Panel — they are present but hidden in Home
Perform an in-place edition upgrade to Windows 11 Pro (e.g., apply a Pro product key)
Reformat and perform a clean install of Windows Home again

explanation.correct: Home→Pro is an in-place edition upgrade (via the Microsoft Store or by changing the product key) that keeps apps, files, and settings while unlocking BitLocker, domain join, and gpedit.

distractors.A: Domain join is an edition capability, not a feature a third-party utility can bolt on.
distractors.B: These features are absent in Home, not merely hidden — nothing to enable.
distractors.D: Reinstalling Home yields the same missing features and wipes the user's data.

explanation.exam_pattern: To gain Pro-only features without a wipe: in-place edition upgrade (change product key / Store). Home never has BitLocker, domain join, or gpedit.

questions.stem: A vendor fix instructs a technician to change a specific value under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE hive. Which built-in Windows tool edits the registry directly?

explanation.correct: regedit opens the registry hives (HKLM, HKCU, etc.) so values can be viewed and edited. Best practice is to export/back up the key before changing it.

distractors.A: Event Viewer displays logged events; it cannot edit the registry.
distractors.B: Disk Management handles partitions and volumes, not registry keys.
distractors.D: Device Manager manages hardware devices and drivers, not registry values.

explanation.exam_pattern: References to HKEY_/hives/registry values → regedit. Back up the key first.

questions.stem: The Print Spooler has stopped. A technician needs to start it again and set it to launch automatically at every boot. Which console is designed for managing this?

explanation.correct: services.msc lists Windows services and lets you start/stop them and set the startup type (Automatic, Manual, Disabled) — exactly what the Print Spooler needs.

distractors.A: Task Scheduler runs programs on a schedule/trigger; it doesn't set a service's startup type.
distractors.B: Performance Monitor graphs performance counters; it doesn't control services.
distractors.D: msinfo32 is a read-only system report — it cannot change service state.

explanation.exam_pattern: Start/stop services and set Automatic/Manual/Disabled startup → services.msc (also reachable from Task Manager's Services tab).

questions.stem: A PC's disk sits at 100% activity. A technician wants a LIVE, per-process view that also shows which specific files each process is reading and writing. Which built-in tool provides this breakdown?

explanation.correct: Resource Monitor shows real-time CPU, Disk, Network, and Memory activity drilled down by process — including the individual files driving disk I/O.

distractors.A: Disk Cleanup deletes temporary files to free space; it doesn't show live I/O.
distractors.B: Registry Editor edits configuration values, not live resource usage.
distractors.C: System Restore rolls the system back to a restore point; it isn't a monitoring tool.

explanation.exam_pattern: Live per-process (and per-file) resource drill-down → Resource Monitor. Historical counters/logs → Performance Monitor.

questions.stem: A technician wants a maintenance script to run automatically every night at 2:00 a.m. Which built-in Windows tool schedules a recurring task like this?

explanation.correct: Task Scheduler creates triggered/recurring jobs — e.g., run a script at 2:00 a.m. daily — without anyone being logged on.

distractors.A: Task Manager shows and ends currently running processes; it can't schedule future runs.
distractors.B: msconfig configures boot and startup options, not scheduled tasks.
distractors.D: Event Viewer reviews logs after the fact; it doesn't launch scheduled jobs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Future/recurring, time- or event-triggered jobs → Task Scheduler. Current processes → Task Manager.

questions.stem: A workstation pulled a bad DHCP lease. From the Windows command line, which TWO commands TOGETHER drop the current lease and request a fresh one? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: ipconfig /release gives up the current DHCP lease; ipconfig /renew then requests a new one from the DHCP server.

distractors.B: /flushdns clears the DNS resolver cache — it has nothing to do with the DHCP lease.
distractors.C: /displaydns just prints the contents of the DNS resolver cache.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP lease cycle = ipconfig /release then /renew. /flushdns and /displaydns act on the DNS cache, not DHCP.

questions.stem: An administrator changed a Group Policy setting and wants a domain workstation to re-apply policy immediately rather than wait for the normal refresh. Which command forces the update?

explanation.correct: gpupdate applies Group Policy now; the /force switch reapplies ALL policy settings instead of only changed ones.

distractors.A: gpresult /r reports which policies HAVE applied (RSoP); it doesn't reapply them.
distractors.B: ipconfig /renew renews a DHCP lease, not Group Policy.
distractors.D: sfc /scannow verifies and repairs protected system files — unrelated to policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Apply policy now = gpupdate (/force to reapply everything). Report what applied = gpresult.

questions.stem: A USB flash drive is stuck in an odd read-only partition state. From the Windows command line, a technician wants to wipe its partition table and recreate it cleanly. Which utility manages disks and partitions from the CLI?

explanation.correct: diskpart is Windows' scriptable partition/volume manager (select disk, clean, create partition, assign) — the right tool to clear and rebuild the layout.

distractors.A: chkdsk checks an existing volume for file-system errors; it doesn't manage partitions.
distractors.B: format writes a file system to an existing volume but doesn't clean/recreate the partition table.
distractors.D: defrag rearranges fragmented files on a volume; it doesn't touch the partition table.

explanation.exam_pattern: Partition/volume management from the CLI (clean, create, assign) → diskpart; chkdsk/format operate WITHIN an existing volume.

questions.stem: At a Linux shell, a user wants to list the contents of the current directory, INCLUDING hidden files whose names begin with a dot. Which command does this?

explanation.correct: ls lists a directory's contents; the -a (all) flag includes hidden dotfiles (e.g., .bashrc) that ls hides by default.

distractors.A: cd changes the current directory; it doesn't list anything.
distractors.B: cat displays (concatenates) the contents of a file, not a directory listing.
distractors.C: pwd prints the current working directory path, not its contents.

explanation.exam_pattern: ls = list directory; -a shows hidden dotfiles; -l adds the long/detailed format.

questions.stem: A Linux administrator needs to find every line that contains the word 'error' inside a large log file. Which command is BEST suited to this text search?

explanation.correct: grep searches text for a pattern and prints matching lines, so 'grep error /var/log/syslog' lists every line containing 'error'.

distractors.A: chmod changes file permissions; 'error' is not a valid permission argument.
distractors.B: kill terminates a process by PID/name; it performs no text search.
distractors.D: ps aux lists running processes, not lines inside a file.

explanation.exam_pattern: Search text for a pattern = grep; pipe other command output into grep to filter it.

questions.stem: A user tries to copy a single 6 GB disk-image file to a USB drive formatted as FAT32 and gets a 'file too large' error, even though the drive shows 50 GB free. What is the cause and the BEST fix?

options.text: The USB drive is failing — replace it
FAT32's 4 GB per-file limit — reformat the drive as exFAT (or NTFS)
The file is corrupt — download it again
USB 2.0 cannot transfer any file larger than 4 GB

explanation.correct: FAT32 cannot store a single file larger than 4 GB regardless of free space. Reformatting as exFAT or NTFS removes that per-file limit.

distractors.A: 50 GB is free and the error is a file-system limit, not a hardware failure.
distractors.C: A size-limit rejection is not file corruption.
distractors.D: USB version affects transfer SPEED, not the maximum file size.

explanation.exam_pattern: FAT32 = 4 GB max single file (and ~32 GB format volume in Windows). exFAT/NTFS remove the 4 GB cap.

questions.stem: A technician initializes a new 6 TB data drive but can only create a usable partition of about 2 TB. Which partition style must the disk use to access the full 6 TB?

options.text: A dynamic disk spanned volume is required

explanation.correct: MBR addresses only ~2 TB, which is why the drive is capped. GPT supports volumes well beyond 2 TB (and up to 128 partitions), so it exposes the full 6 TB.

distractors.B: MBR is the CAUSE of the 2 TB cap, not the fix.
distractors.C: FAT32 is a file system, not a partition style — it doesn't change the 2 TB disk limit.
distractors.D: Spanning isn't needed; GPT alone addresses the whole single disk.

explanation.exam_pattern: MBR = 2 TB and 4 primary partitions max. GPT = >2 TB and up to 128 partitions (UEFI required to BOOT from GPT).

questions.stem: A technician remotely connects to \\PC01\C$ and reaches the entire C: drive of that machine. What kind of share is C$?

options.text: A normal user share visible to everyone who browses the PC

explanation.correct: C$ is a default hidden administrative share (the $ hides it from browsing) that maps the root of the C: drive and requires administrative credentials.

distractors.A: C$ is a disk share of the volume root, not a printer.
distractors.B: HomeGroup was a deprecated consumer sharing feature, unrelated to admin shares.
distractors.D: The trailing $ hides it from normal browsing, and only administrators can use it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default hidden admin shares end in $ (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$): hidden from browsing and usable only with administrative credentials.

questions.stem: A user must set per-user file and folder PERMISSIONS and turn on file-level ENCRYPTION on a local volume. Which file system supports these features?

explanation.correct: Only NTFS provides file/folder permissions, EFS encryption, compression, and journaling — the features the user needs.

distractors.A: FAT32 has no file-level permissions or encryption.
distractors.C: CDFS is the read-only file system for optical discs.
distractors.D: exFAT is built for flash-media interchange and also lacks permissions/encryption.

explanation.exam_pattern: Permissions + EFS encryption + compression + journaling = NTFS only; FAT32/exFAT are 'dumb' interchange file systems.

questions.stem: Before performing a CLEAN installation of Windows on an existing PC, which point must the technician make clear to the user?

options.text: A clean install only changes the Windows edition
A clean install keeps all installed programs and settings
A backup is never required for a clean install
A clean install erases the OS, apps, and data on the target partition — back up first

explanation.correct: A clean install wipes the target partition and starts fresh, so anything on it is lost unless backed up first.

distractors.A: Changing the edition is an edition upgrade, not a clean install.
distractors.B: Keeping apps/settings describes an in-place upgrade or repair install, not a clean install.
distractors.C: Because the target partition is wiped, backing up the user's data is essential.

explanation.exam_pattern: Clean install = wipe target partition (fresh start). In-place upgrade/repair = keep apps, files, and settings.

questions.stem: A technician must start Windows Setup on a PC with a completely blank drive. Which TWO are valid installation BOOT methods? (Choose two.)

options.text: Network (PXE) boot from a deployment server
Boot from a bootable USB flash drive

explanation.correct: Install media can be launched from a bootable USB drive or over the network via PXE — both work on a blank drive with no OS present.

distractors.B: Safe Mode boots an ALREADY-installed Windows for troubleshooting; it is not an install source.
distractors.C: System Restore rolls back an installed system to a restore point; it can't install Windows.

explanation.exam_pattern: Install boot methods: USB, optical, external drive, network/PXE. Safe Mode and System Restore act on an already-installed OS.

questions.stem: A Windows 10 PC with a fast CPU and plenty of RAM is refused the Windows 11 upgrade. Which firmware/security requirement, newly required by Windows 11, MOST often blocks otherwise-capable machines?

explanation.correct: Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0 and UEFI Secure Boot; these are frequently present but disabled in firmware, which is why capable PCs fail the check until they're enabled.

distractors.A: Windows uses NTFS for its system partition; a FAT32 system partition isn't a requirement.
