distractors.B: Windows 11 is 64-bit only — a 32-bit CPU can't run it at all, let alone 'satisfy' a requirement.
distractors.D: Windows 11 requires UEFI, so legacy BIOS/CSM is the opposite of what's needed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Windows 11 floor: UEFI + Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, 64-bit supported CPU, 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage.

questions.stem: During installation a technician can choose a quick format or a full format of the target drive. What does a FULL format do that a quick format does not?

options.text: It encrypts the volume with BitLocker
It automatically installs the device drivers
It scans the disk for bad sectors (and more thoroughly clears the volume)
It converts the disk from MBR to GPT

explanation.correct: A full format writes a fresh file system AND scans every sector for bad spots (and overwrites the volume on modern Windows); a quick format just rewrites the file table, so it's much faster but skips the sector check.

distractors.A: Formatting does not enable BitLocker encryption.
distractors.B: Formatting never installs drivers.
distractors.D: Partition style (MBR vs. GPT) is chosen separately; the format type doesn't convert it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Quick format = rewrite file table only (fast). Full format = also scan for bad sectors and clear the volume (slow).

questions.stem: A networked printer needs a fixed address, so a technician must assign a static IPv4 address, subnet mask, and default gateway to a Windows PC. Where is this configured?

options.text: In the adapter's Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4) properties

explanation.correct: Static addressing is set in the network adapter's TCP/IPv4 properties — IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers.

distractors.A: Disk Management handles partitions and volumes, not IP configuration.
distractors.B: Device Manager manages the adapter's driver/hardware, not its IP settings.
distractors.D: Task Manager's Performance tab only graphs throughput; it can't set an address.

explanation.exam_pattern: Static IP/DNS → adapter properties → TCP/IPv4. Blank/automatic = DHCP; DHCP failure yields an APIPA 169.254.x.x address.

questions.stem: Company policy routes all web traffic through a proxy server at 10.0.0.5 port 8080. On a Windows client, where is the proxy server configured?

explanation.correct: The Windows proxy is set under Network & Internet > Proxy, either manually (host:port) or via an automatic configuration script.

distractors.A: Disk Management manages partitions/volumes.
distractors.B: Event Viewer reviews logs; it doesn't configure networking.
distractors.D: Device Manager manages hardware and drivers, not web-proxy settings.

explanation.exam_pattern: Windows proxy → Settings > Network & Internet > Proxy (manual host:port or auto-config script).

questions.stem: A remote user must securely reach the corporate LAN over the public Internet from a Windows laptop. Which Windows networking feature establishes this encrypted connection to the company gateway?

options.text: A VPN connection (Settings > Network & Internet > VPN)

explanation.correct: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel across the Internet into the private LAN; it's added under Network & Internet > VPN with the server address and authentication.

distractors.A: A mapped drive points to a share but provides no secure tunnel on its own.
distractors.C: A metered connection just flags data-usage limits; it doesn't create a tunnel.
distractors.D: Airplane mode disables the radios — the opposite of connecting.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encrypted tunnel over the Internet into the private network = VPN (Network & Internet > VPN).

questions.stem: A user tethers a Windows laptop to a cellular hotspot with a capped data plan and wants Windows to limit background data and defer large updates on that network. Which setting should be enabled for the connection?

options.text: Toggle the network between Public and Private repeatedly

explanation.correct: Marking a connection as metered tells Windows to reduce background data and hold back large downloads/updates on that network — ideal for capped cellular plans.

distractors.B: Remote Desktop is unrelated to limiting data usage.
distractors.C: Disabling the adapter ends connectivity entirely.
distractors.D: The location profile controls discovery/firewall behavior, not data caps.

explanation.exam_pattern: Capped/cellular link → set it as a metered connection to throttle background data and large updates.

questions.stem: On macOS, which built-in utility securely stores a user's website passwords, Wi-Fi keys, and certificates?

explanation.correct: Keychain Access is the macOS encrypted store for passwords, Wi-Fi keys, and certificates.

distractors.A: Mission Control arranges open windows and virtual desktops (Spaces).
distractors.C: Spotlight is the system-wide search feature.
distractors.D: Time Machine is the macOS backup/restore utility.

explanation.exam_pattern: macOS: Keychain = credential/cert store; Time Machine = backup; Spotlight = search; Mission Control = window/Spaces manager.

questions.stem: A Mac user needs to erase and reformat an external drive and run First Aid to repair directory errors on it. Which built-in macOS tool does this?

explanation.correct: Disk Utility formats, partitions, and erases volumes and runs First Aid to repair disk/directory errors on macOS.

distractors.A: Keychain Access stores credentials, not disk tools.
distractors.B: The App Store installs applications; it doesn't manage disks.
distractors.D: Finder browses files and folders but can't format a volume or run First Aid.

explanation.exam_pattern: macOS Disk Utility ≈ Windows Disk Management + chkdsk: format/partition/erase plus First Aid repair.

questions.stem: A user with an Intel-based Mac wants to install Windows and dual-boot it NATIVELY alongside macOS. Which Apple utility is designed for this?

explanation.correct: Boot Camp Assistant partitions the disk and installs Windows so an Intel Mac can dual-boot it natively (not in a virtual machine).

distractors.A: Time Machine backs up and restores files.
distractors.B: FileVault encrypts the macOS startup disk.
distractors.D: Gatekeeper controls which app sources are allowed to run.

explanation.exam_pattern: Native Windows dual-boot on an Intel Mac = Boot Camp (partition + install Windows). Apple Silicon Macs don't support Boot Camp.

questions.stem: On Linux, a standard user must run a single command that requires root privileges (for example, installing a package) and gets 'permission denied.' Which command runs just that command as the superuser?

explanation.correct: Prefixing a command with sudo runs that one command with root (superuser) privileges, after the user authenticates.

distractors.A: man opens a command's manual page.
distractors.B: ls lists directory contents.
distractors.C: pwd prints the current directory path.

explanation.exam_pattern: sudo = run ONE command as root; su = switch to the root (or another) user's shell for a session.

questions.stem: An administrator wants a batch file to run automatically each time a domain user logs on — mapping drives and configuring printers. Which Active Directory feature delivers this?

options.text: A logon script applied through Group Policy

explanation.correct: A logon script (delivered via Group Policy) runs automatically at user logon to map drives, set printers, and apply environment settings.

distractors.A: Folder redirection points folders like Documents to a server share; it doesn't run a script.
distractors.C: A local account isn't managed by AD/Group Policy, so no domain logon script applies.
distractors.D: BitLocker encrypts the drive; it has nothing to do with logon automation.

explanation.exam_pattern: AD/Group Policy tools: logon scripts (run at logon), folder redirection, home folder, OUs, and security groups.

questions.stem: After signing in to Windows once in the morning, a user can open the intranet, email, and the HR portal without re-entering credentials for each. Which concept provides this?

explanation.correct: SSO lets one authenticated identity access many services without repeated logins — one sign-on, many apps.

distractors.A: A hardware token is an MFA device, not the single-sign-on mechanism itself.
distractors.B: Least privilege limits what an account may do; it isn't about avoiding repeated logins.
distractors.D: MFA adds a second factor, which means MORE prompts, not fewer, and is a different concept.

explanation.exam_pattern: Authenticate once, reach many services = SSO (convenience/identity). Adding factors = MFA (assurance).

questions.stem: To deter theft of laptops in an open retail office, which inexpensive PHYSICAL control secures each laptop to the desk?

explanation.correct: A cable lock physically tethers the laptop to a desk or fixture, deterring walk-off theft of the hardware.

distractors.A: A password protects login, not the physical removal of the laptop.
distractors.B: BitLocker protects the DATA if stolen but doesn't prevent the physical theft.
distractors.C: A firewall filters network traffic; it does nothing to stop someone carrying the device away.

explanation.exam_pattern: Physical theft deterrents = cable/equipment locks, server/USB locks. Encryption and passwords protect DATA, not the device's presence.

questions.stem: A secure lab door unlocks only after scanning an employee's fingerprint. Which authentication FACTOR does the fingerprint represent?

explanation.correct: A fingerprint is a biometric — 'something you are.'

distractors.B: 'Something you know' is a password or PIN.
distractors.C: 'Somewhere you are' is a location-based factor (e.g., GPS/geofencing).
distractors.D: 'Something you have' is a token, smart card, or phone.

explanation.exam_pattern: Factor types: know (password), have (token/card), are (biometric), plus somewhere-you-are. Combine DIFFERENT types for MFA.

questions.stem: A piece of malware spreads by itself from PC to PC across the network with no user action, consuming bandwidth as it replicates. Which type is it?

explanation.correct: A worm self-replicates and spreads across hosts/networks on its own, without needing a user to run it.

distractors.A: A keylogger records keystrokes; it doesn't self-propagate.
distractors.B: A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and requires the user to run it.
distractors.D: Ransomware encrypts data for payment — it's defined by extortion, not self-spread.

explanation.exam_pattern: Self-replicating + spreads with no user interaction = worm. Needs a user/host to run = virus/trojan.

questions.stem: A user's banking passwords are stolen even though they never shared their screen. Investigation finds software secretly recording every keystroke and sending it to an attacker. Which malware is this?

explanation.correct: Secretly capturing keystrokes to harvest credentials is the definition of a keylogger (a form of spyware).

distractors.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment.
distractors.C: A worm self-propagates across hosts; it isn't specifically a keystroke recorder.
distractors.D: A rootkit hides at a privileged level to maintain stealthy access; capturing keystrokes isn't its defining trait.

explanation.exam_pattern: Records keystrokes to steal credentials = keylogger/spyware. Hides to keep privileged access = rootkit.

questions.stem: In CompTIA's best-practice malware removal procedure, which TWO actions involve System Restore on a Windows PC? (Choose two.)

options.text: Permanently disable System Restore on all company PCs
Disable System Restore BEFORE remediating the malware
Roll the PC back from a restore point as the very first troubleshooting step
Re-enable System Restore and create a new restore point AFTER cleaning

explanation.correct: You disable System Restore before remediation (old restore points can harbor the malware) and re-enable it with a fresh restore point once the system is clean.

distractors.A: System Restore is re-enabled afterward, not permanently disabled.
distractors.C: The process starts by identifying/verifying symptoms and quarantining — not by rolling back (a restore point could reinfect the PC).

explanation.exam_pattern: 7 steps: 1 identify/verify symptoms → 2 quarantine → 3 disable System Restore → 4 remediate (update + scan/remove) → 5 schedule scans/updates → 6 re-enable System Restore + make a restore point → 7 educate the user.

questions.stem: While remediating an infected Windows PC, a stubborn malware process keeps relaunching in normal mode and prevents the anti-malware scan from finishing. Which technique is recommended to complete the removal?

options.text: Grant the user's account local administrator rights
Boot into Safe Mode (or a preinstallation/recovery environment) and run the scan there
Disable the antivirus so Windows starts faster

explanation.correct: Starting in Safe Mode (or booting a preinstallation/recovery environment) keeps the malware from auto-launching, so the anti-malware scan can run and remove it.

distractors.A: Giving the account admin rights raises risk and doesn't stop the process relaunching.
distractors.C: Turning off updates leaves the PC more vulnerable and doesn't remove the malware.
distractors.D: Disabling the antivirus removes the very tool needed to clean the system.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remediation = update anti-malware definitions + use scanning/removal techniques; for stubborn infections boot Safe Mode or a preinstallation/recovery environment.

questions.stem: Thousands of employees receive an email appearing to come from 'IT Support' with a link to a fake login page urging them to 'verify your password now.' Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: A mass deceptive email trying to harvest credentials via a fake page is phishing.

distractors.A: Whaling targets a specific high-value executive, not a mass audience.
distractors.B: A DDoS floods a service to deny availability; it isn't credential trickery.
distractors.D: Tailgating is physically following someone through a secured door.

explanation.exam_pattern: Mass deceptive email for credentials = phishing. A single targeted exec = whaling; a targeted individual/group = spear phishing.

questions.stem: An employee receives a TEXT MESSAGE claiming a package is being held and they must tap a link to pay a small fee, which asks for card details. Which social-engineering attack is this?

explanation.correct: Phishing delivered by SMS/text message is smishing.

distractors.B: Vishing is phishing over a voice phone call.
distractors.C: An evil twin is a rogue Wi-Fi access point impersonating a legitimate SSID.
distractors.D: Shoulder surfing is watching someone enter sensitive data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phishing by channel: email = phishing, SMS/text = smishing, voice call = vishing.

questions.stem: In a busy airport, an attacker stands close behind a traveler and watches them type their laptop password and PIN. Which technique is this, and what is a simple countermeasure?

options.text: Shoulder surfing — use a privacy screen filter and shield entry
Tailgating — install an access control vestibule
Dumpster diving — shred documents before disposal

explanation.correct: Directly observing someone entering credentials is shoulder surfing; privacy filters, positioning, and shielding entry mitigate it.

distractors.B: Phishing is deceptive messaging, not visual observation.
distractors.C: Tailgating is following someone through a secured door.
distractors.D: Dumpster diving is scavenging discarded media/paper for information.

explanation.exam_pattern: Watching credential entry over the shoulder = shoulder surfing → privacy filter + awareness + positioning.

questions.stem: An attacker scatters USB flash drives labeled 'Payroll 2026' in the company parking lot, hoping an employee plugs one in and runs the malware it carries. Which social-engineering technique is this?

explanation.correct: Leaving tempting infected media for a curious victim to pick up and use is baiting. Disabling AutoRun and endpoint controls helps mitigate it.

distractors.A: Whaling targets an executive, typically by email.
distractors.C: Vishing uses a voice phone call.
distractors.D: An on-path attack intercepts traffic between two parties; it isn't a dropped-media lure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Leaving infected media/links for a victim to take = baiting → disable AutoRun/AutoPlay and use endpoint control.

questions.stem: To limit the damage malware can do, which type of account should employees use for their DAY-TO-DAY work on a Windows PC?

explanation.correct: Daily work should use a standard account so malware runs with limited rights; elevate via UAC/Run as administrator only when a task truly needs it.

distractors.B: A guest account is too limited for real work and should be disabled, not used daily.
distractors.C: Running as administrator lets malware make system-wide changes with no prompt barrier.
distractors.D: Domain controller service accounts are server infrastructure, not user logins.

explanation.exam_pattern: Least privilege: everyday use = standard account; elevate (UAC / Run as administrator) only when required.

questions.stem: Windows Defender Firewall applies a different set of rules depending on the network the PC is connected to. Which set of PROFILES does it use?

explanation.correct: Windows Defender Firewall has three network profiles — Domain, Private, and Public — each with its own inbound/outbound rules.

distractors.A: Home/Work/School are not the firewall's profile names.
distractors.B: Red/Yellow/Green is not a Windows firewall concept.
distractors.D: Inbound/Outbound are rule directions WITHIN each profile, not the profiles themselves.

explanation.exam_pattern: Defender Firewall profiles: Domain (AD network), Private (trusted LAN/home), Public (untrusted) — each with its own ruleset.

questions.stem: On a standalone Windows 11 PC with no third-party antivirus installed, which BUILT-IN component provides real-time malware protection?

explanation.correct: Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the built-in real-time anti-malware engine in Windows; it protects the PC when no third-party AV is present.

distractors.A: UAC gates privilege elevation; it doesn't detect or remove malware.
distractors.B: The firewall filters network connections; it isn't a file/malware scanner.
distractors.D: BitLocker encrypts the drive at rest — it doesn't scan for malware.

explanation.exam_pattern: Built-in Windows roles: Defender Antivirus = real-time AV; Firewall = traffic filter; BitLocker = encryption; UAC = privilege gate.

questions.stem: Clinic staff keep walking away leaving their sessions open. Which hardening setting BEST prevents a passerby from using an unattended, logged-in workstation?

options.text: A screen lock that activates after a short idle period and requires the password to resume

explanation.correct: An inactivity screen lock (requiring the password to resume) stops a passerby from using a session the user walked away from.

distractors.B: CPU speed has nothing to do with securing an unattended session.
distractors.C: Disabling the firewall weakens security and does nothing about physical walk-up access.
distractors.D: A screen saver without a password lock still lets anyone move the mouse and continue.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unattended workstation → auto screen lock + short timeout (and Win+L to lock manually).

questions.stem: To slow down automated password-guessing (brute-force) attacks against local accounts, which policy should a technician configure?

options.text: An account lockout threshold that locks the account after a set number of failed logons

explanation.correct: An account lockout threshold locks the account after N failed attempts, throttling brute-force guessing.

distractors.A: Enabling AutoPlay is a malware vector — it weakens security, not strengthens it.
distractors.C: Shorter passwords are weaker and easier to guess, the opposite of hardening.
distractors.D: A screen-saver timeout governs idle locking, not failed-logon attempts.

explanation.exam_pattern: Throttle brute force with a lockout threshold + duration; pair with password length/complexity and MFA.

questions.stem: As an account-management hardening measure, a company wants to ensure shift workers cannot log on to their workstations OUTSIDE their scheduled shift hours. Which setting accomplishes this?

options.text: Configure logon time restrictions (permitted logon hours) on the user accounts
Grant all shift workers local administrator rights
Enable AutoPlay for removable media after hours

explanation.correct: Logon time restrictions (permitted logon hours) block sign-in outside the allowed window, enforcing when each account may be used.

distractors.B: Granting admin rights weakens security and doesn't limit when users can log on.
distractors.C: AutoPlay is a malware vector and has nothing to do with restricting hours.
distractors.D: Disabling the lockout policy removes brute-force protection — it reduces security.

explanation.exam_pattern: Account-management hardening: restrict logon hours/times, set lockout thresholds and screen-lock timeouts, enforce least privilege, and disable/rename default accounts.

questions.stem: A technician performs a standard (quick) format on a hard drive before donating the PC and assumes the data is gone. Why is this UNSAFE for sensitive data?

options.text: A quick format permanently encrypts the data
A standard format only clears the file table; the underlying data is still recoverable with tools
Formatting physically destroys the drive platters

explanation.correct: A standard/quick format just resets the file system's index; the actual data remains on the platters and can be recovered with widely available tools.

distractors.A: Formatting doesn't encrypt anything.
distractors.C: Formatting is a logical operation; it does not physically harm the platters.
distractors.D: Formatting has nothing to do with magnetic degaussing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Quick/standard format is recoverable. For reuse → multi-pass drive wipe/overwrite; for disposal → physical destruction.

questions.stem: A batch of solid-state drives (SSDs) will be REUSED internally and must be sanitized so prior data cannot be recovered. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Waving a strong magnet over each SSD to overwrite it
ATA Secure Erase using the SSD's built-in sanitize command (or the vendor's tool)

explanation.correct: SSDs are sanitized for reuse with ATA Secure Erase (or the manufacturer's secure-erase utility), which clears the flash cells using the drive's own command set.

distractors.A: Degaussing only affects MAGNETIC media; it does nothing to flash-based SSDs.
distractors.B: Magnets don't erase flash memory — this isn't a real sanitization method.
distractors.C: A standard format leaves data recoverable.

explanation.exam_pattern: SSD sanitize for reuse = ATA Secure Erase / vendor tool. Degaussing works only on magnetic HDDs and tape, NOT on SSDs.

questions.stem: Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field to sanitize media. On which TWO types of media is degaussing EFFECTIVE? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Degaussing scrambles the magnetic fields that store data, so it works on magnetic HDDs and magnetic tape.

distractors.A: SSDs store data in flash cells, which a magnetic field does not erase.
distractors.B: Optical discs store data optically (pits/dye), not magnetically, so degaussing has no effect.

explanation.exam_pattern: Degaussing = magnetic media only (HDDs, tape). SSDs need secure erase; optical media must be shredded/physically destroyed.

questions.stem: Users on a workstation suddenly cannot print, and the technician finds the Print Spooler service is not running. Which built-in console should be used to start the service AND set its startup type so it launches automatically at every boot?

explanation.correct: The Services console (services.msc) lists Windows services, lets you start/stop them, and lets you set the Startup type (Automatic/Manual/Disabled) so the Print Spooler comes back on its own at boot.

distractors.A: Disk Management handles partitions and volumes, not service state or startup type.
distractors.B: Event Viewer shows logs that can tell you WHY a service stopped, but it cannot start the service or change its startup type.
distractors.D: Device Manager manages hardware devices and their drivers, not Windows services.

explanation.exam_pattern: Start/stop a Windows service and set its startup type = Services console (services.msc); Task Manager's Services tab can only start/stop, not configure startup.

questions.stem: A PC is sluggish and shows 100% disk usage. The technician wants to see, in real time, exactly which process and which file are driving the disk I/O (not just an overall percentage). Which built-in tool gives this detailed per-process breakdown?

explanation.correct: Resource Monitor breaks CPU, disk, network, and memory usage down per process — including which files/handles a process is reading or writing — so you can pinpoint the exact cause of the disk thrashing.

distractors.A: Registry Editor edits configuration keys; it is not a performance-monitoring tool.
distractors.C: Disk Cleanup deletes temporary files to reclaim space; it shows no live resource usage.
distractors.D: System Restore rolls the system back to an earlier point; it does not display live I/O.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detailed live per-process CPU/disk/network/memory (which file/handle) = Resource Monitor; a quick overview or 'end task' = Task Manager.

questions.stem: A user who keeps many applications and dozens of browser tabs open repeatedly sees 'Your computer is low on memory' warnings, and the system slows to a crawl. Which action BEST addresses the low-memory condition?

options.text: Run Disk Cleanup to delete temporary files
Close unneeded programs and either add physical RAM or increase the virtual-memory (page file) size

explanation.correct: Low-memory errors mean RAM (plus page file) is exhausted. Close unneeded programs, add more physical RAM, and/or increase the page file (virtual memory) so Windows has more room to work.

distractors.A: Display resolution has a negligible effect on system RAM pressure.
distractors.B: Disk Cleanup frees disk SPACE, which is not the same as memory — it won't stop low-RAM warnings.
distractors.D: Defragmenting reorganizes files on disk for access speed; it adds no memory.

explanation.exam_pattern: Low-memory errors -> close apps, add RAM, or enlarge the page file (virtual memory); free disk space is NOT free memory.

questions.stem: A single installed desktop application crashes immediately on launch, while every other program and the OS run normally. After confirming the app is fully updated, what is the BEST next step to fix just that one application?

options.text: Repair or reinstall that application, and check Event Viewer for the faulting module
Perform a clean reinstall of the entire Windows OS

explanation.correct: When one app misbehaves but the OS and other apps are fine, the problem is scoped to that app. Repair it (or uninstall and reinstall it), and use Event Viewer's Application log to identify the faulting module if needed.

distractors.A: Replacing the drive is a hardware action with no evidence of hardware failure here.
distractors.C: A graphics-driver rollback addresses display/BSOD issues, not one application failing to start.
distractors.D: Reinstalling all of Windows is wildly out of proportion to a single broken application.

explanation.exam_pattern: One app crashes while the OS/other apps are fine -> update, then repair/reinstall that app; read Event Viewer for the faulting module.

questions.stem: After several improper shutdowns, Windows reports file-system errors on the C: volume and some files fail to open with read errors, yet the drive's SMART status is healthy. Which command checks and repairs LOGICAL file-system errors on the volume?

options.text: chkdsk C: /f  (add /r to also locate bad sectors)

explanation.correct: chkdsk with /f fixes file-system structure errors (lost clusters, cross-linked files, a dirty volume); /r additionally scans for and recovers from bad sectors. Logical corruption after improper shutdowns is exactly what chkdsk repairs.

distractors.A: sfc /scannow repairs protected Windows SYSTEM files, not the file-system structures on the volume.
distractors.B: diskpart clean erases the partition table and all data on the disk — destructive and wrong here.
distractors.C: ipconfig /flushdns clears the DNS resolver cache and has nothing to do with disk file systems.

explanation.exam_pattern: Logical file-system/volume errors -> chkdsk /f (/r for bad sectors); sfc/DISM repair OS files, not the file system.

questions.stem: A user signs in and lands on a blank 'temporary' desktop with none of their files or settings. Event Viewer logs 'The User Profile Service failed the sign-in. User profile cannot be loaded.' Each reboot repeats it. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Reinstall the last application the user opened
Rebuild the user's Windows profile — back up their data, then repair the profile (correct the ProfileList registry reference or create a fresh profile) and migrate the files in

explanation.correct: A temporary profile with 'User Profile Service failed the sign-in' means the user's profile is corrupt or its ProfileList reference is broken. Back up the user's data, then rebuild the profile (fix the registry reference or create a new profile) and copy the data back.

distractors.A: A corrupt profile is a software/account issue; nothing points to a failed motherboard.
distractors.B: Windows Update is unrelated to a corrupt local user profile.
distractors.C: The failure happens at sign-in before apps load, so reinstalling an app does not address it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Temporary profile / 'User Profile Service failed the sign-in' -> rebuild the Windows user profile (fix ProfileList or new profile, then migrate data).

questions.stem: A user's browser home page and default search engine changed on their own, unfamiliar toolbars appeared, and ad pop-ups now load on almost every site — and the changes return after being reset. What is the BEST remediation?

options.text: Change the default search engine and ignore the pop-ups
Disable HTTPS so pages load faster
Remove the malicious browser extensions and any PUP (potentially unwanted program), reset the browser settings, then run a reputable anti-malware scan

explanation.correct: A hijacked home page/search, rogue toolbars, and ad pop-ups are classic adware/PUP symptoms. Remove the offending extensions and program, reset the browser, and run an anti-malware scan so the changes don't keep coming back.

distractors.A: Just switching the search engine leaves the adware installed, so the hijack recurs.
distractors.B: Disabling HTTPS weakens security and does nothing to remove the unwanted software.
distractors.C: Cache size has nothing to do with a browser hijack; it won't remove the adware.

explanation.exam_pattern: Browser hijack/redirect + pop-ups/toolbars = adware/PUP -> remove extensions/PUP, reset the browser, scan with anti-malware.

questions.stem: A user's documents now carry a strange new extension and won't open, and a full-screen note demands cryptocurrency payment within 48 hours for a decryption key. What is the BEST course of action?

options.text: Do not pay; isolate the machine from the network, remove the malware (or reimage), restore the files from a known-good backup, and report the incident
Run Disk Defragmenter to rebuild the scrambled files
Rename the files back to their original extensions
Pay the ransom immediately so the files are released

explanation.correct: This is ransomware. Paying funds criminals with no guarantee of recovery. Isolate the host to stop spread, remove the malware or reimage, restore data from a clean backup, and report through the proper channels.

distractors.B: Defragmentation reorganizes files on disk; it cannot reverse encryption.
distractors.C: The data is encrypted, not merely renamed — changing the extension back does nothing.
distractors.D: Paying is discouraged — it funds attackers and often does not restore the data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ransomware (encrypted files + ransom note) -> don't pay; isolate, remove/reimage, restore from backup, and report.

questions.stem: Malware on a PC prevents the installed antivirus from launching or updating, and it closes the installer for a replacement tool as soon as it opens. Which approach BEST lets the technician scan and remove the malware?

options.text: Keep retrying the same antivirus in normal mode until it finally opens
Boot into Safe Mode (or use a bootable antivirus / the Windows preinstallation recovery environment) so the malware is inactive, then run an updated scan
Delete the System32 folder to remove the infected files
Disable the firewall so the antivirus can update

explanation.correct: When malware blocks security tools, start the system in an environment where the malware isn't running — Safe Mode, a bootable AV rescue disk, or a preinstallation/recovery environment — then run an updated scan so the tool can actually remove it.

distractors.A: If the malware blocks the AV in normal mode, repeating the attempt will keep failing.
distractors.C: Deleting System32 destroys Windows itself — catastrophic, not a remediation.
distractors.D: Turning off the firewall lowers protection and does not stop the malware from blocking the AV.

explanation.exam_pattern: Malware blocks your AV -> scan from Safe Mode or a bootable/preinstallation environment (malware inactive), then remove.

questions.stem: A technician has removed the malware from a PC, confirmed it is clean, updated the anti-malware definitions, and re-enabled System Restore with a fresh restore point. According to CompTIA's best-practice malware-removal procedure, what is the FINAL step?

options.text: Educate the end user about safe browsing, email caution, and updates to help prevent reinfection
Investigate and verify the malware symptoms

explanation.correct: The seven-step procedure ends with educating the end user, so the behavior that led to the infection is less likely to repeat.

distractors.B: Disabling System Restore is an early step (step 3); it has already been handled and re-enabled.
distractors.C: Investigating/verifying symptoms is the FIRST step, already completed here.
distractors.D: Quarantining the system is an EARLY step (step 2), done right after verifying symptoms.

explanation.exam_pattern: Malware 7 steps: Investigate -> Quarantine -> Disable System Restore -> Remediate -> Schedule scans/update -> Re-enable System Restore -> EDUCATE the end user (last).

questions.stem: Every device on a small office network is being redirected to convincing fake look-alike sites. The technician checks several PCs and finds each one's hosts file is clean and the system clocks are correct. Where is the redirection MOST likely configured?

options.text: The keyboard language settings on each PC
The firmware of the users' monitors
Malware changed the router's/DHCP DNS server settings, so every client resolves names through a rogue DNS server
The hosts file on each individual PC

explanation.correct: When the WHOLE network is redirected but the per-PC hosts files are clean, the common point is the router: malware has pointed its DNS (handed out by DHCP) at a rogue server, so all clients get poisoned answers. Reset the router's DNS and credentials and update its firmware.

distractors.A: Keyboard language settings have nothing to do with DNS or site redirection.
distractors.B: Monitors display output; their firmware plays no part in name resolution.
distractors.D: The hosts files were verified clean, and a hosts-file attack would have to be repeated on every single PC — not the likely cause of a network-wide redirect.

explanation.exam_pattern: One PC redirected -> check its hosts file; the WHOLE network redirected (hosts files clean) -> check the router/DHCP DNS for a rogue DNS server.

questions.stem: After returning from international travel, a user's phone shows 'No Service' and cannot use cellular data, although Wi-Fi works normally. Which is the BEST first troubleshooting step?

options.text: Perform a full factory reset of the phone
Toggle Airplane mode off/on (or restart) to re-register on the carrier, and verify cellular data/roaming and the correct APN are enabled; reset network settings if it persists

explanation.correct: 'No Service' after travel is usually a registration/roaming/APN issue. Toggling Airplane mode or restarting forces the phone to re-register; confirm cellular data and roaming are on and the APN is correct, and reset network settings if needed — all before anything drastic.

distractors.A: Clearing the browser cache does not restore cellular service.
distractors.B: A screen swap is a hardware repair unrelated to cellular registration.
distractors.C: A factory reset wipes the device and is far too drastic as a first step for a radio-registration issue.

explanation.exam_pattern: No cellular service -> toggle Airplane mode/restart to re-register, check roaming/APN, then reset network settings; factory reset only as a last resort.

questions.stem: A user cannot install or update apps; the phone reports 'insufficient storage available,' and the camera also refuses to save new photos. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Upgrade to a faster cellular data plan
Free up storage — clear app caches, remove unused apps, and offload photos/media (or add/clean an SD card where supported)

explanation.correct: 'Insufficient storage' means internal storage is full. Clear caches, delete unused apps, and move photos/media to the cloud or an SD card so apps can install/update and the camera can save again.

distractors.A: Turning off Bluetooth frees no storage.
distractors.B: Data-plan speed is unrelated to how much storage the device has free.
distractors.C: Battery condition affects runtime, not available storage space.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Insufficient storage' / can't update or save -> free space (clear caches, remove unused apps, offload media, add/clean SD).

questions.stem: A user notices the camera/microphone indicator turning on by itself and finds an unfamiliar app that has been granted camera, microphone, location, and contacts access. Which TWO actions BEST remediate this likely spyware? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run a reputable mobile anti-malware scan and review what else the app accessed or installed
Revoke the app's unnecessary permissions and uninstall the suspicious app

explanation.correct: Unauthorized camera/microphone/location activity by an unknown app is a spyware symptom. Revoke its permissions and uninstall it, then run a mobile anti-malware scan and review what it reached, so nothing it dropped is left behind.

distractors.A: Auto-rotate is a display setting and does nothing to stop unauthorized access.
distractors.B: Screen-timeout length is a display/power setting with no effect on spyware.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unauthorized camera/mic/location access by an app = mobile spyware -> revoke permissions/uninstall + anti-malware scan and review access (avoid unofficial app sources).

questions.stem: A navigation app repeatedly places a user far from their real position and intermittently reports 'GPS signal lost,' while other phones nearby locate correctly. Which step is MOST likely to resolve it?

options.text: Enable high-accuracy Location services and grant the app location permission, then toggle Location (or restart) to reacquire a fix

explanation.correct: Poor/incorrect location is usually a Location-services setting or permission problem. Turn on high-accuracy location, make sure the app has location permission, and toggle Location or restart so the device reacquires a satellite fix.

distractors.A: Disabling mobile data removes assisted-GPS data and does not fix the fix problem.
distractors.C: Ringtone volume has nothing to do with GPS positioning.
distractors.D: The SIM provides cellular identity/service, not GPS positioning.

explanation.exam_pattern: GPS inaccurate / 'signal lost' -> enable high-accuracy Location + app permission, toggle/restart to reacquire; a clear view of the sky helps.

questions.stem: Which document defines the rules employees must follow when using company computers, email, and the Internet — for example, prohibiting personal peer-to-peer downloads and non-work use of company systems?

explanation.correct: An acceptable use policy (AUP) states what employees may and may not do with company resources — devices, email, and Internet access.

distractors.A: An SOP is the step-by-step 'how we perform a task' document, not a usage-rules policy.
distractors.B: A topology diagram maps how devices connect on the network.
distractors.D: An incident report records the details of a specific event after it occurs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rules for how employees may use company resources = AUP; step-by-step task instructions = SOP.

questions.stem: Before planning a switch replacement, a technician wants documentation that shows how the network's devices and segments are interconnected. Which document provides this?

explanation.correct: A network topology diagram depicts how devices and network segments connect (physically and/or logically), which is what you need when planning or troubleshooting connectivity.

distractors.B: A knowledge base article documents a known issue and its fix, not the network layout.
distractors.C: An asset tag is an inventory label on a single device, not a map of the network.
distractors.D: A password policy defines credential rules, not network connections.

explanation.exam_pattern: How devices/segments interconnect = network topology diagram (physical and/or logical).

questions.stem: When an employee leaves the company, IT follows a documented list of tasks: disable the user's accounts, revoke building and VPN access, and collect issued devices. What is this document BEST called?

options.text: An end-user termination (offboarding) checklist — a standard operating procedure

explanation.correct: A documented set of consistent steps for processing a departing employee is an end-user termination (offboarding) checklist — a type of SOP that ensures access is revoked and assets are recovered every time.

distractors.A: A EULA states the legal terms for using software.
distractors.C: An incident report documents a specific security/operational event.
distractors.D: A change request is a proposal to modify a system, not an offboarding procedure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Steps for staff leaving = end-user termination checklist; for staff joining = new-user setup checklist (both are SOPs).

questions.stem: A change request must list exactly which servers, applications, and user groups the change will touch. Which element of the change request is this?

explanation.correct: The scope defines the boundaries of the change — which systems, applications, and users it affects — so everyone understands its reach.

distractors.B: End-user acceptance is the affected users agreeing they have reviewed and are ready for the change.
distractors.C: The rollback/back-out plan describes how to revert if the change fails, not what it touches.
distractors.D: The purpose explains WHY the change is being made.

explanation.exam_pattern: Which systems/users are affected = scope; how to undo = rollback plan; why = purpose.

questions.stem: Before approval, the change team evaluates how likely the change is to cause problems and how severe the impact would be, then labels it low, medium, or high. Which change-request element is this?

explanation.correct: Weighing likelihood and impact and assigning a low/medium/high rating is the risk analysis / risk level — it helps the change board decide and prioritize.

distractors.A: The rollback plan is the documented reversal procedure if the change fails.
distractors.B: The responsible staff member is the person accountable for performing the change.
distractors.D: Sandbox testing validates the change in an isolated environment; it is not the risk rating itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: Assess likelihood + impact and rate it low/med/high = risk analysis / risk level.

questions.stem: A formal change request names the specific person who is accountable for carrying out the change and overseeing its outcome. Which element does this represent?

explanation.correct: Documented business processes identify a responsible staff member — the individual accountable for performing the change and seeing it through.

distractors.B: Affected end users are those impacted by the change, not the person accountable for executing it.
distractors.C: The backout plan is the procedure for reverting a failed change.
distractors.D: The CAB is the GROUP that reviews and approves/rejects the change, not the individual performing it.

explanation.exam_pattern: The named individual accountable for performing/overseeing a change = responsible staff member (part of documented business processes).

questions.stem: Which backup type copies ALL selected data every time it runs and allows the simplest, fastest restore because only that one backup set is needed?

explanation.correct: A full backup copies all selected data on every run, so a restore needs only that single set — the simplest, fastest recovery, at the cost of the longest backup time and most storage.

distractors.A: A synthetic full is assembled from existing backups on the backup server, not a fresh copy of all source data.
distractors.C: A differential copies changes since the last FULL; a restore needs the full plus the latest differential.
distractors.D: An incremental copies only changes since the last backup of any type; a restore needs the full PLUS every increment in order.

explanation.exam_pattern: Full = copies everything each run; simplest/fastest restore (one set), slowest backup, most storage.

questions.stem: A business takes a FULL backup every Sunday and a DIFFERENTIAL backup each weekday evening. To fully restore the data on Thursday morning, which backups are required?

options.text: Sunday's full backup plus Wednesday evening's (the most recent) differential — two sets
Sunday's full plus every weekday differential, applied in order

explanation.correct: A differential holds everything changed since the last FULL, so a restore needs just the full plus the single most recent differential — Sunday's full and Wednesday evening's differential.

distractors.A: The full alone misses all changes made Monday through Wednesday.
distractors.B: A differential cannot restore on its own; it must be applied on top of the full backup.
distractors.D: Applying every differential in order is how INCREMENTAL chains restore — differentials need only the latest one.

explanation.exam_pattern: Differential restore = last full + the single latest differential. Incremental restore = last full + EVERY incremental since.

questions.stem: To avoid the long nightly transfer of a full backup across the network, a backup server merges the last full backup with all later incrementals into a brand-new full backup on the backup storage itself — without re-reading all the data from the client. What is the resulting backup called?

explanation.correct: A synthetic full is produced on the backup server by combining an existing full with the subsequent incrementals, giving a new full-equivalent restore point without a fresh full read from the source.

distractors.A: A differential captures changes since the last full, read from the client — it is not assembled from other backups.
distractors.B: An incremental captures only changes since the last backup, read from the client.
distractors.D: 3-2-1 is a copies/media/off-site guideline, not a type of backup produced by merging.

explanation.exam_pattern: Synthetic full = a full assembled on the backup server from an existing full + increments (no full re-read from the source).

questions.stem: When servicing the inside of a power supply unit (PSU) or a CRT monitor, technicians are specifically told NOT to wear a grounded anti-static wrist strap. Why?

options.text: The wrist strap would generate static electricity that damages the PSU
These components store a dangerous high-voltage charge in their capacitors; a grounded strap could channel that charge through the technician and cause severe shock
PSUs and CRTs are immune to ESD, so a strap is merely unnecessary
The wrist strap simply slows the technician down

explanation.correct: PSUs and CRTs hold a lethal stored charge in their capacitors even when unplugged. A grounded wrist strap gives that high voltage a path through you, so the strap is a shock hazard here — these units should only be opened by trained personnel.

distractors.A: A wrist strap prevents static buildup; it does not generate it. The real danger here is stored high voltage.
distractors.C: The reason is the stored high-voltage shock hazard to the technician, not that the devices are 'immune' to ESD.
distractors.D: Speed is not the issue — the concern is a potentially fatal electrical shock.

explanation.exam_pattern: Never wear a grounded ESD strap inside a PSU or CRT — stored high-voltage/capacitor charge is a potentially lethal shock hazard.

questions.stem: A server room experiences frequent brief voltage sags (brownouts) and occasional blackouts that reboot the servers. Which device BOTH keeps the servers running through a sag or outage AND conditions the power?

options.text: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) with battery backup and AVR

explanation.correct: A UPS supplies battery power through sags and outages and, with automatic voltage regulation (AVR), conditions the incoming power — keeping servers up long enough to ride through or shut down cleanly.

distractors.A: A power strip merely adds outlets and provides no power protection at all.
distractors.B: A KVM switch shares one keyboard/monitor/mouse among computers; it does nothing for power.
distractors.D: A surge suppressor only clamps voltage spikes; it has no battery, so it cannot carry a load through a brownout or blackout.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ride through brownouts/blackouts + conditioning = UPS (battery + AVR); a surge suppressor only stops spikes.

questions.stem: A technician must clean thick dust out of dozens of PCs in a dusty warehouse. Which practice BEST protects the technician from inhaling the airborne particles?

options.text: Wear an air-filtration mask and blow out the dust with compressed air (or an ESD-safe vacuum) in a well-ventilated area
Keep a Class C fire extinguisher nearby

explanation.correct: Dust is an inhalation hazard, so wear an air-filtration mask (respirator) and clear the dust with compressed air or an ESD-safe vacuum in a ventilated space.

distractors.A: Cut-resistant gloves guard against cuts, not inhaled particles.
distractors.B: An anti-static strap prevents ESD damage to components; it does nothing to protect the lungs.
distractors.D: A Class C extinguisher is for energized electrical fires — unrelated to dust inhalation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Airborne particulates/dust -> air-filtration mask (PPE) + compressed air/ESD vacuum in a ventilated area.

questions.stem: A hard drive may hold evidence for a legal case. To preserve it, what should the technician create and then work from, leaving the original drive untouched?

options.text: A ZIP archive of the user's visible documents
A quick-formatted clone that skips 'empty' space to save time
A bit-for-bit forensic image (copy) of the drive, verified with a hash to prove integrity

explanation.correct: Preserving evidence means capturing a bit-for-bit forensic image (including deleted and slack space), hashing it to prove it was not altered, and analyzing the COPY while the original is secured under chain of custody.

distractors.A: A System Restore point reverts Windows settings; it is not an evidence copy of the drive.
distractors.B: Zipping only the visible documents misses deleted/hidden data and does not preserve integrity.
distractors.C: A quick format and skipping unallocated space discards recoverable evidence — it is not a forensic copy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Preserve evidence -> bit-for-bit forensic image, hash it, analyze the COPY; keep the original and chain of custody intact.

questions.stem: A spreadsheet contains employees' full names, Social Security numbers, and home addresses. Which category of regulated data is this?

explanation.correct: Names, Social Security numbers, and addresses identify a specific person, making this personally identifiable information (PII), which must be handled and protected accordingly.

distractors.A: PHI is medical/health information specifically (e.g., diagnoses, treatment records).
distractors.C: Public records are already published and are not sensitive, regulated data.
distractors.D: PCI is cardholder/payment card account data governed by PCI DSS.

explanation.exam_pattern: Identity data (name/SSN/address) = PII; medical = PHI; card data = PCI; EU personal data = GDPR.

questions.stem: A company serving customers in the European Union must honor requests to erase personal data and must notify authorities of a data breach within strict timeframes. Which regulation imposes these requirements?

explanation.correct: The GDPR governs personal data of EU residents, granting rights such as erasure and requiring timely breach notification — making it the regulation described.

distractors.A: An SLA is a service-level agreement defining performance metrics between parties.
distractors.B: PCI DSS is a payment-card security standard, not an EU personal-data privacy law.
distractors.D: A EULA states the legal terms for using a piece of software.

explanation.exam_pattern: EU personal-data rights (erasure, breach notification) = GDPR; card data = PCI DSS.

questions.stem: Midway through a repair, a technician realizes it will take two days longer than the estimate already given to the customer. What is the MOST professional action?

options.text: Blame the parts supplier and the customer's old equipment
Say nothing and hope it is finished before the customer notices
Quietly return the device unrepaired to avoid an awkward conversation
Proactively contact the customer, explain the delay, give a realistic new timeline, and offer options

explanation.correct: Setting and MEETING expectations means communicating status proactively: tell the customer about the delay, provide a realistic revised timeline, and offer options so they can decide how to proceed.

distractors.A: Shifting blame is unprofessional and does nothing to help the customer.
distractors.B: Going silent fails to manage expectations and erodes trust when the deadline passes.
distractors.C: Returning the device unrepaired abandons the job and the customer entirely.

explanation.exam_pattern: Set and MEET expectations: communicate status proactively, give a realistic timeline, offer options, and follow up.

questions.stem: When dealing with a difficult or argumentative customer, which TWO behaviors are MOST professional? (Choose two.)

options.text: Dismiss the problem as minor so the customer calms down
Raise your voice to match the customer's tone so they take you seriously
Do not argue with the customer or become defensive
Ask open-ended, clarifying questions and restate the issue to confirm your understanding

explanation.correct: With a difficult customer, avoid arguing or getting defensive, and use clarifying, open-ended questions plus a restatement of the issue to show you understand and to de-escalate.

distractors.A: Minimizing or dismissing the problem is dismissive and unprofessional, and usually makes things worse.
distractors.B: Matching the customer's raised voice escalates the conflict rather than resolving it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Difficult customers: don't argue/get defensive, don't minimize or dismiss, avoid being judgmental; clarify and restate to confirm understanding.

questions.stem: A technician needs a simple script of sequential Command Prompt commands that runs natively on Windows with no extra interpreter installed. Which file type is the BEST fit?

explanation.correct: A .bat (or .cmd) batch file runs a sequence of Command Prompt commands natively on Windows with nothing extra to install.

distractors.B: .sh is a Linux/Unix Bash shell script and does not run natively in Windows Command Prompt.
distractors.C: .vbs is a VBScript file — a different Windows scripting language, not a Command Prompt batch file.
distractors.D: .py requires the Python interpreter to be installed.

explanation.exam_pattern: .bat/.cmd = native Windows batch | .ps1 PowerShell | .sh Bash | .py Python | .vbs VBScript | .js JavaScript.

questions.stem: An administrator wants ONE scripting language to run the same automation on Windows, Linux, AND macOS, with a large library ecosystem for tasks like parsing files and calling web APIs. Which is the BEST choice?

explanation.correct: Python runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS and has a vast standard and third-party library ecosystem, making it the best single cross-platform choice for general automation.

distractors.A: Batch files run only in the Windows Command Prompt.
distractors.B: Bash is the Unix/Linux (and macOS) shell and does not run natively on Windows without an added layer.
distractors.D: VBScript is a legacy Windows-only scripting language.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cross-platform, general-purpose scripting with rich libraries = Python (.py); .bat/.vbs are Windows-only and .sh is Unix/Linux/macOS.

questions.stem: Which TWO tasks are appropriate to automate with a script? (Choose two.)

options.text: Collect a hardware and software inventory from each machine into a report
Silently install the same application on dozens of workstations
Physically reseat a loose RAM module

explanation.correct: Scripts shine at repeatable software tasks — pushing an application install to many PCs and gathering inventory/data from each machine are classic use cases.

distractors.B: Replacing a screen is a physical repair, not something a script can do.
distractors.D: Reseating RAM is a hands-on hardware task a script cannot perform.

explanation.exam_pattern: Script use cases: app installation, remap drives, restart machines, automated backups, gather info, initiate updates — never physical hardware repairs.

questions.stem: A data center installs a small two-door room at its entrance: the outer door must close and the person be verified before the inner door will open, specifically to prevent an unauthorized person from slipping in behind an employee. What is this physical control called?

explanation.correct: An access control vestibule (formerly 'mantrap') is a two-door area that lets only one verified person through at a time, directly preventing tailgating/piggybacking.

distractors.A: A bollard is a short, sturdy post that blocks vehicles from an area; it doesn't control pedestrian entry one person at a time.
distractors.B: A badge reader authenticates a credential at a door, but by itself does nothing to stop a second person from following through the open door.
distractors.C: A cable lock physically tethers a laptop to a desk to deter theft; it isn't an entry-control mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Two interlocking doors passing one verified person = access control vestibule (mantrap), the countermeasure to tailgating.

questions.stem: In an Active Directory domain, an administrator wants each user's Documents folder to physically reside on a network file server so it is backed up centrally and follows the user to any domain PC they sign in to. Which feature accomplishes this transparently?

explanation.correct: Folder redirection (configured via Group Policy) transparently points known folders such as Documents and Desktop to a network location, so the data is centrally stored/backed up and available wherever the user logs in.

distractors.A: A home folder is a designated per-user network storage location (often mapped to a drive letter), but it doesn't transparently redirect the Documents known folder itself.
distractors.C: A login script runs commands (e.g., maps drives, sets printers) at sign-in; it doesn't relocate the Documents known folder to the server.
distractors.D: A security group is a collection of accounts used to assign permissions; it has nothing to do with relocating a user's folders.

explanation.exam_pattern: Documents/Desktop transparently stored on the server = folder redirection; mapped personal drive = home folder; run-at-logon commands = login script.

questions.stem: Company policy states that every user account and service should be granted only the minimum rights required to do its job, and no more. Which security principle does this describe?

explanation.correct: The principle of least privilege grants each user, process, or service only the minimum access needed to perform its function, limiting the damage from mistakes or compromise.

distractors.A: Implicit deny means anything not explicitly permitted is blocked (a common default on ACLs/firewalls); it's a default-deny rule, not the idea of minimizing each account's rights.
distractors.B: An ACL is a list defining which subjects may access a resource — a mechanism that can enforce least privilege, but not the principle itself.
distractors.D: MAC is an access-control model using labels/clearances assigned by the system; it's a model, not the minimize-rights principle.

explanation.exam_pattern: Give only the minimum rights needed = least privilege; 'deny unless explicitly allowed' = implicit deny.

questions.stem: For multifactor authentication, a company issues each employee a small physical keyfob that displays a rotating six-digit one-time code. What category of authentication device is the keyfob?

explanation.correct: A hard token is a dedicated hardware device that generates one-time passcodes (e.g., an RSA-style keyfob); it's a 'something you have' factor independent of the user's phone or PC.

distractors.A: A soft token is software-based — an authenticator app running on a phone or computer; the standalone hardware keyfob described is a hard token.
distractors.B: A smart card is a physical card with an embedded chip that must be inserted into or tapped on a reader; it doesn't display a rotating numeric code the way an OTP keyfob does.
distractors.D: A biometric factor is 'something you are' (fingerprint, face, iris); a code-generating keyfob measures nothing about the person.

explanation.exam_pattern: Dedicated hardware OTP device = hard token; authenticator app = soft token; both are 'something you have.'

questions.stem: A user installs what looks like a free PDF utility, but hidden inside, the program quietly opens a backdoor that lets an attacker control the PC remotely. The malware does not self-replicate. Which type of malware is this?

explanation.correct: A trojan (Trojan horse) disguises itself as legitimate, desirable software to trick the user into installing it, then performs malicious actions such as opening a backdoor. It does not self-replicate.

distractors.B: A worm self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, with no need to masquerade as a wanted program or for the user to run it.
distractors.C: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment; the described malware grants stealthy remote access rather than ransoming data.
distractors.D: A boot sector virus infects the disk's boot sector/MBR so it loads before the OS; it isn't a disguised downloadable utility.

explanation.exam_pattern: Disguised as legit software + user-installed + no self-replication = trojan; self-spreading over a network = worm.

questions.stem: A technician is following CompTIA's best-practice procedure for malware removal. They have already (1) investigated and verified the malware symptoms and (2) quarantined the infected system. According to the recommended order, what should they do NEXT?

options.text: Remediate the system — update anti-malware and scan/remove

explanation.correct: CompTIA's order is: 1) investigate/verify symptoms, 2) quarantine, 3) DISABLE System Restore (Windows), 4) remediate (update anti-malware, then scan and remove), 5) schedule scans and run updates, 6) re-enable System Restore and create a restore point, 7) educate the end user. After quarantining, step 3 is to disable System Restore so infected restore points can't reinfect the system.

distractors.A: Educating the end user is the FINAL step (7), done once the system is clean.
distractors.B: Scheduling scans and running updates is step 5, performed after remediation.
distractors.C: Remediation (update anti-malware and scan/remove) is step 4 — it comes AFTER disabling System Restore, not before.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order: verify -> quarantine -> disable System Restore -> remediate -> schedule scans/updates -> re-enable System Restore -> educate the user.

questions.stem: Malware on a workstation operates at a privileged (kernel) level, actively hides its own files, processes, and registry keys from the OS and antivirus, and standard scans in normal Windows fail to detect it. Which type of malware is this?

explanation.correct: A rootkit embeds itself at a privileged level and conceals its presence from the OS and security tools, making detection and removal difficult; remediation often needs offline scanning, a pre-boot environment, or OS reinstallation.

distractors.A: Spyware covertly collects information about the user and their activity; it isn't defined by kernel-level stealth and privileged concealment.
distractors.B: Adware displays unwanted advertisements; it's a nuisance, not stealthy privileged code.
distractors.D: A keylogger records keystrokes to capture credentials; it may run hidden, but its defining trait is logging input, not kernel-level self-concealment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hides at privileged/kernel level and evades AV = rootkit; may require an offline/pre-boot scan or a reimage to remove.

questions.stem: Several PCs have suddenly become sluggish, their fans run at full speed, and CPU/GPU utilization sits near 100% even when idle; monitoring shows outbound connections to a mining pool. Which type of malware is MOST likely present?

explanation.correct: A cryptominer (cryptojacking malware) hijacks a system's CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker, which shows up as very high processor/GPU usage, heat, fan noise, and sluggishness, plus traffic to mining pools.

distractors.A: A rootkit hides malware; a cryptominer may use rootkit techniques, but the symptoms here (maxed CPU/GPU plus mining-pool traffic) specifically point to a cryptominer.
distractors.B: A keylogger quietly records keystrokes; it uses negligible resources and wouldn't peg the CPU/GPU at full load.
distractors.C: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment; it causes a brief spike during encryption, not sustained full-load mining with pool connections.

explanation.exam_pattern: Sustained near-100% CPU/GPU, heat/fans, and mining-pool traffic = cryptominer/cryptojacking.

questions.stem: An attacker crafts a highly targeted email aimed specifically at the company's CFO, impersonating the CEO and urgently requesting a large wire transfer. The message is tailored to that one high-level executive. Which attack BEST describes this?

explanation.correct: Whaling is a phishing attack that targets a 'big fish' — a high-profile executive such as a CEO or CFO — with a message tailored to them, often to authorize fraudulent transfers.

distractors.A: Spear phishing targets a specific individual or group; whaling is the specialized subset aimed at a senior executive, which best fits targeting the CFO.
distractors.B: Shoulder surfing is covertly watching someone enter credentials or data; no observation is involved here.
distractors.C: Vishing is voice/telephone-based social engineering; this attack arrives by email.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phishing aimed at a high-level executive = whaling; tailored to a specific ordinary individual = spear phishing; generic mass email = phishing.

questions.stem: A user receives a phone call from someone claiming to be the bank's fraud department, pressuring them to read back their account number and PIN 'to stop a fraudulent charge.' Which social-engineering attack is this?

explanation.correct: Vishing (voice phishing) uses a phone call to manipulate the victim into revealing sensitive information such as account numbers or PINs.

distractors.A: Smishing is phishing via SMS/text messages; this attack came over a voice call, not a text.
distractors.C: Shoulder surfing is directly observing someone enter information; the attacker here never watches the victim.
distractors.D: Whaling targets high-profile executives specifically; the victim here is an ordinary account holder.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phone call tricking you out of info = vishing; text message = smishing; email = phishing.

questions.stem: In a coffee shop, an attacker sets up a rogue wireless access point broadcasting the same SSID as the shop's legitimate Wi-Fi, hoping customers connect to it so their traffic can be intercepted. What is this attack called?

explanation.correct: An evil twin is a rogue wireless access point that mimics a legitimate network's SSID to lure victims into connecting, allowing the attacker to intercept or manipulate their traffic.

distractors.A: Shoulder surfing is secretly watching someone enter credentials or data; it doesn't involve a fake access point.
distractors.C: Tailgating is physically following an authorized person through a secured door; it isn't a wireless attack.
distractors.D: Dumpster diving is searching discarded trash for useful information; no network is involved.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rogue AP cloning a real SSID to lure clients = evil twin.

questions.stem: An attacker recovers discarded printouts, old account statements, and sticky notes with passwords from a company's unsecured trash bins to gather information for an attack. Which social-engineering technique is this?

explanation.correct: Dumpster diving is sifting through an organization's discarded trash to find sensitive information (documents, credentials, configurations) that can aid an attack; shredding/secure disposal is the countermeasure.

distractors.A: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured entry; it's about physical entry, not scavenging trash.
distractors.B: Impersonation is pretending to be someone (e.g., IT support) to manipulate a victim; no direct interaction occurs in dumpster diving.
distractors.C: Phishing uses fraudulent electronic messages to trick victims; dumpster diving is a physical information-gathering technique.

explanation.exam_pattern: Harvesting info from the trash = dumpster diving; prevent it with shredding/secure disposal.

questions.stem: A company requires that any data copied to USB flash drives be encrypted so a lost drive's contents cannot be read. Which built-in Windows feature is designed specifically for this?

explanation.correct: BitLocker To Go is the Windows feature that encrypts removable drives (USB flash drives, external disks), requiring a password or key to unlock them on any PC.

distractors.A: Defender Antivirus scans for and removes malware; it provides no drive encryption at all.
distractors.B: EFS encrypts individual files/folders per user on an NTFS volume; it isn't the feature built to encrypt whole removable drives.
distractors.C: Standard BitLocker encrypts fixed internal volumes/the OS drive, not removable USB media — that's the To Go variant.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encrypt removable/USB drives = BitLocker To Go; fixed/OS volume = BitLocker; per-file on NTFS = EFS.

questions.stem: When a user tries to install a program, Windows dims the screen and displays a prompt asking for consent or an administrator password before the system-level change is allowed. Which security feature is this?

explanation.correct: User Account Control (UAC) prompts for consent or administrator credentials before an action that requires elevated privileges, preventing silent system changes by malware or standard users.

distractors.A: Windows Defender Firewall filters network traffic; it has nothing to do with the elevation prompt.
distractors.C: BitLocker encrypts drives; it doesn't produce an elevation consent prompt.
distractors.D: SmartScreen warns about unrecognized downloaded apps and malicious sites; it doesn't gate local privilege elevation for every system change.

explanation.exam_pattern: Dimmed screen + consent/admin-password prompt before a system change = UAC.

questions.stem: Using only built-in Windows tools, a technician needs to create a rule that blocks inbound connections on a specific TCP port. Which tool should they configure?

explanation.correct: Windows Defender Firewall (with Advanced Security) creates inbound and outbound rules that allow or block traffic by port, protocol, program, or address.

distractors.B: SmartScreen checks the reputation of downloaded apps and websites; it doesn't block traffic on specific ports.
distractors.C: BitLocker encrypts drives and has no role in filtering network traffic.
distractors.D: Defender Antivirus detects and removes malware; it does not create port-based network rules.

explanation.exam_pattern: Allow/block traffic by port/program = Defender Firewall; detect/remove malware = Defender Antivirus.

questions.stem: Which TWO built-in Windows features protect data at rest by encrypting it? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: BitLocker encrypts entire volumes and EFS encrypts individual files/folders on NTFS — both provide encryption of data at rest.

distractors.A: UAC controls privilege elevation with consent prompts; it does not encrypt any data.
distractors.D: SmartScreen checks the reputation of downloaded apps/websites to warn about threats; it provides no encryption.

explanation.exam_pattern: Windows data-at-rest encryption = BitLocker (whole volume) + EFS (per file/folder); UAC and SmartScreen don't encrypt.

questions.stem: To stop users from changing the boot order or booting from external media to bypass Windows security on lab PCs, which hardening measure should a technician apply?

options.text: Enable BitLocker To Go on all USB drives
Add all users to the local Administrators group

explanation.correct: A BIOS/UEFI supervisor (setup) password prevents unauthorized users from changing firmware settings such as boot order or enabling external boot, which would otherwise let them bypass the OS and its protections.

distractors.A: BitLocker To Go encrypts removable drives; it doesn't stop someone from changing the firmware boot order.
distractors.B: Disabling the firewall removes a protective control — it weakens security rather than hardening it.
distractors.D: Adding users to Administrators violates least privilege and makes the system less secure, not more.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lock down boot order / external boot = BIOS/UEFI (supervisor) password.

questions.stem: A technician is configuring a password policy to harden user accounts. Which TWO settings reflect password best practices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set passwords to expire and require periodic change
Require a minimum length and complexity (mix of character types)
Store all user passwords in a shared spreadsheet for recovery
Disable account lockout so users are never locked out

explanation.correct: Enforcing a minimum length with complexity and requiring periodic expiration/change are standard password-hardening practices that resist guessing and limit how long a compromised password stays useful.

distractors.C: Storing passwords in a shared spreadsheet exposes every credential at once — a severe security failure, not a best practice.
distractors.D: Disabling account lockout lets attackers brute-force passwords with unlimited attempts; lockout thresholds should be ENABLED.

explanation.exam_pattern: Harden passwords: length + complexity, expiration, history, and account lockout; never store them in plaintext or remove lockout.

questions.stem: As part of account-management hardening on a new workstation, which action follows best practice?

options.text: Give every user membership in the Administrators group
Keep the manufacturer's default credentials on the device
Rename the default Administrator account and disable the Guest account
Leave the Guest account enabled for convenience

explanation.correct: Renaming the built-in Administrator account (so attackers can't target a known name) and disabling the Guest account reduce the attack surface — core account-management hardening steps.

distractors.A: Making every user an administrator violates least privilege and lets any user or their malware alter the system.
distractors.B: Keeping default credentials is a well-known risk; default usernames/passwords should always be changed.
distractors.D: Leaving Guest enabled provides an anonymous, low-control foothold; it should be disabled.

explanation.exam_pattern: Account hardening: rename/secure the default admin, disable Guest, change default credentials, apply least privilege.

questions.stem: Which ongoing practice BEST protects workstations against exploitation of newly discovered operating-system and application vulnerabilities?

options.text: Running as a local administrator at all times
Disabling automatic updates to avoid reboots
Patch/update management — keep the OS and applications current

explanation.correct: Patch (update) management — regularly applying OS and application updates/security patches — closes known vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them, and is a fundamental hardening practice.

distractors.A: Running as administrator all the time violates least privilege and lets malware make system-wide changes.
distractors.B: Turning off the host firewall removes a protective control and exposes the machine to network attacks.
distractors.C: Disabling automatic updates leaves known vulnerabilities unpatched, directly increasing risk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Close known vulnerabilities = patch/update management; pair it with least privilege and a host firewall.

questions.stem: A company wants to permanently destroy the data on failed magnetic hard disk drives by exposing them to a powerful magnetic field. Which sanitization method is this?

explanation.correct: Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field to scramble the magnetic domains on a hard disk drive, destroying the data (and usually the drive). It works only on magnetic media.

distractors.A: A standard/quick format only clears the file table and leaves the underlying data recoverable — it isn't secure destruction.
distractors.C: A low-level format rewrites the drive's low-level structures but uses no magnetic field; it's a software/firmware operation and the term is often misused for a full overwrite.
distractors.D: Secure erase issues a firmware command to wipe a drive's cells (useful for SSDs/HDDs being kept for reuse); it's not a magnetic-field method.

explanation.exam_pattern: Strong magnetic field wiping a magnetic HDD = degaussing (no effect on SSDs/flash, which have no magnetic domains).

questions.stem: A drive will NOT be reused and its data must be physically destroyed. Which TWO are physical destruction methods? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deleting the files and emptying the Recycle Bin
Drilling or hammering through the platters
